passages.title: Veiled hearts and the answer they are given
passages.tafsir:
These eight ayat open the sūrah by describing what the Qur'an is — where it came from, how clearly it speaks, what it does to people — and then let the Quraysh answer back in their own words. That confrontation holds the passage together: a Book sent down by the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful, in their own language, met with "our hearts are veiled" — followed by Allah's instruction to His Messenger ﷺ on how to reply.

## Ḥā Mīm, and a revelation from mercy (ayat 1–2)

Ayah 1 is simply **Ḥā Mīm**. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān notes that seven sūrahs begin this way, and the scholars came to speak of them as a group — *al-Ḥawāmīm*; since they share an opening, extra words were attached to tell them apart, and this sūrah is known as *Ḥā Mīm Sajdah* or *Ḥā Mīm Fuṣṣilat*. Ibn Kathir does not pause on the letters themselves; he reads ayat 1 and 2 as one statement — the Qur'an is sent down from the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.

**Tanzīl** means a sending-down, and ayah 2 says from Whom: *ar-Raḥmān ar-Raḥīm*. Ibn Kathir sets this beside "Say: Rūḥ al-Qudus (Jibrīl) has brought it down from your Lord with truth" (16:102) and "this is a revelation from the Lord of all that exists, which the trustworthy Rūḥ has brought down upon your heart that you may be one of the warners" (26:192–194).

Notice which Names are chosen. The sūrah is about to record hard refusal and pronounce woe on those who associate partners with Allah — yet the Book carrying all of that is introduced as coming *from mercy*. The warning of ayah 4 and the woe of ayah 6 belong to that same sending-down.

## "Its āyāt are explained in detail" (ayah 3)

Ayah 3 gives the Book three descriptions. The first is *fuṣṣilat āyātuhu*. Ibn Kathir glosses it: its meanings are clear and its rulings are sound and wise.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān opens the word further. *Fuṣṣilat* is from *faṣl*, which originally means **distinguishing things by separating them**. So it means stating matters very clearly by explaining them in detail — either by separating them subject by subject, or by gathering them in one place. The Qur'an's distinct subjects — the injunctions of the Sharīʿah, the stories, the beliefs, the refutation of people of false beliefs — are each set out in their own right, and each explained with examples too. This is not a book that says everything at once in a blur; it takes things apart so they can be seen.

The second description is *qurʼānan ʿarabiyyan* — **an Arabic Qur'an**. Ibn Kathir: because it is a clear Arabic Qur'an, its meanings are precise and detailed and its words are clear and not confusing. He compares 11:1, "a Book, the āyāt whereof are completed, and then explained in detail from One Who is All-Wise" — meaning, he says, that it is miraculous in its wording *and* in its meanings. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān presses the point at the first audience: the Quraysh received it *in their own language*, so that they would have no difficulty understanding it.

The third phrase, **li-qawmin yaʿlamūn** — "for people who know" — Ibn Kathir takes to mean that this clear style will be readily understood by scholars thoroughly versed in knowledge. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān draws out the other side: all this clarity can only benefit those who *intend* to ponder over it and understand it.

## Glad tidings, warning, and the turning away (ayah 4)

**Bashīran wa nadhīran.** Ibn Kathir: sometimes it brings glad tidings to the believers, sometimes warning to the disbelievers. Then the sentence turns: *most of them turned away, so they do not hear.* Ibn Kathir comments that most of the Quraysh did not understand anything of it at all — **despite the fact that it was so clear**. They had witnessed the marvel of the Qur'an, says Maʿārif ul Qurʼān, and had seen innumerable miracles of the Prophet ﷺ, and still turned away; they would not even bear to listen. Note the order too: "so they hear not" comes *after* "they turned away". The not-hearing is the consequence, not the excuse.

## The day ʿUtbah came to negotiate

The most illuminating thing about these ayat is an incident Maʿārif ul Qurʼān records at length. The Quraysh had first tried to crush Islam by force, hurting the Messenger of Allah ﷺ and those who believed with him in every way they could. It did not work; the circle of believers kept widening. Powerful men entered Islam — Sayyidnā ʿUmar ibn al-Khaṭṭāb, then Sayyidnā Ḥamzah, one of the recognised leaders of Quraysh. So Makkah changed tactics: perhaps persuasion and temptation would block the road that intimidation had not.

On the sources: Ḥāfiẓ Ibn Kathir reproduces the incident from the *Musnad* of Bazzār, from Abū Yaʿlā and from Baghawī — considering Baghawī's nearest to the truth — and then from *Kitāb as-Sīrah* of Muhammad ibn Isḥāq, preferring that to the other three. Ibn Isḥāq's version follows, from Muhammad ibn Kaʿb al-Quraẓī, who had the report from ʿUtbah ibn Rabīʿah himself, a foremost leader of Quraysh.

One day ʿUtbah was sitting in al-Masjid al-Ḥarām with a group of Quraysh, while the Messenger of Allah ﷺ sat alone in a corner on the other side. ʿUtbah said: if you agree, let me talk to Muhammad ﷺ and offer him some attractions — if he accepts, we give them to him, and he stops preaching against our religion. His men answered with one voice: *O Abūʼl-Walīd, do it — please talk to him.*

ʿUtbah went over. "O nephew, you know that you are high-born and a noble man of the Quraysh, and your family is respected by all of us. But you have put the tribe in great difficulty. You have given a call that has created divisions among us, made us look like fools, stigmatised our deities and our religion, and declared our forefathers to be disbelievers. So listen to me — I will put a few things to you, and you may choose among them." The Prophet ﷺ said, "Go ahead; I am listening."

The offer came in four parts. If your aim is wealth, we will gather so much for you that you will be the richest man of the nation. If it is leadership, we will take you as leader of the whole of Quraysh and do nothing without your order. If you want kingship, we accept you as our king. And if some jinn or devil comes to you and compels you to this and you cannot drive him off, we will have you treated at our own expense.

ʿUtbah went on at some length, and the Prophet ﷺ kept listening. When he finished, the Prophet ﷺ asked, "Have you finished?" He said yes. "Now please listen to me." ʿUtbah replied, "No doubt, I would listen to you."

And then — instead of answering with an argument of his own — the Prophet ﷺ began to recite **this sūrah**: *Bismillāhi ar-Raḥmāni ar-Raḥīm. Ḥā Mīm. A revelation from the All-Merciful, the Very-Merciful — a Book whose verses are elaborated in the form of an Arabic Qur'an for a people who understand.*

Two endings to the recitation are reported. Bazzār and Baghawī narrate that at a later point in the sūrah ʿUtbah put his hand over the blessed mouth of the Prophet ﷺ and begged him, by their kinship, to recite no further for their sake. Ibn Isḥāq narrates that ʿUtbah listened quietly and attentively, propping himself on his hands behind his back, until the Prophet ﷺ reached the āyah of prostration in this sūrah and prostrated. Then he turned to ʿUtbah: "You have heard what you heard, and now you are free to do what you like."

ʿUtbah walked back. Seeing him coming, his companions said among themselves: *by Allah, Abūʼl-Walīd's face has changed — it is not the face that left us.* They asked what news he brought. He said: "I heard such a discourse that, by Allah, I have never heard anything like it before; by Allah, it is neither a sorcerer's enchantment, nor a poet's poetry, nor a soothsayer's incantation. O Quraysh, listen to me. Leave off confronting him and let him go about his business, for this discourse of his is bound to attain eminence. Wait and see how the rest of Arabia deals with them. If the other Arabs defeat them, your problem is solved without effort on your part; and if he prevails over the Arabs, then his rule is your rule, his honour your honour, and you will be the luckiest of people because of him." (Ibn Kathir, vol. 4, p. 91)

Hearing this they said: "O Abūʼl-Walīd, Muhammad has cast an enchanting spell upon you with his words." ʿUtbah answered: "I have given you my advice; now do what you like."

Read ayah 4 again with that scene in front of you. ʿUtbah *heard* — enough to declare publicly that it was not magic, not poetry, not soothsaying — and his own tribe answered with the very accusation he had just refuted.

## "Our hearts are veiled" (ayah 5)

Ayah 5 records three excuses in one breath, which Maʿārif ul Qurʼān numbers: a cover on their hearts against his discourse, so they do not understand him; deaf ears; barriers between him and them. Ibn Kathir's glosses are blunt: their hearts are wrapped and screened; 'we are deaf to the message you bring us'; 'nothing of what you say reaches us.' And the closing line, *so work you; verily we are working*, means: go your way and we will go ours, and we will not follow you.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān adds an important reading of their tone: this was not a report from men who had genuinely lost hearing and intellect — **it was a kind of ridicule and jest they used to make**. It was also a plea of helplessness: curtained hearts, leaden ears, a wall between — so how could we possibly listen?

### The apparent conflict with 6:25

Elsewhere Allah says of such people: "But We have put coverings on their hearts, so that they do not understand, and heaviness in their ears" (6:25) — almost the words the disbelievers use here. Yet in ayah 5 the Qur'an reproduces their statement **in the context of denouncing it**, which shows the statement is false. Is there a conflict?

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān answers (citing *Bayān ul-Qurʼān*): when the disbelievers said it, they meant they were helpless and therefore excusable. When the Qur'an says it in Sūrah al-Anʿām, it does not treat them as helpless at all — it holds them fully capable of hearing and understanding. Only when they refused even to hear, and had no intention of understanding, were heedlessness and ignorance imposed on them **as a punishment** — and not to a degree that stripped them of their will; had they changed their minds even then, their abilities of hearing and understanding would have been restored fully.

The veil is real, but it is earned — and it is not a locked door.

## The answer the Prophet ﷺ was told to give (ayah 6)

They mocked; the reply commanded in ayah 6 does not mock back. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān draws attention to this: the response to their ridicule was not to be offensive in kind, but to express humility — that he ﷺ is not a deity holding authority over everything, but a human being, the only difference being that his Lord has given him guidance through *waḥy* (revelation) and supported him with miracles. That alone should have brought them to faith.

Ibn Kathir walks the ayah through. **"I am only a human being like you; it is revealed to me that the One you must worship is One alone"** — not like these idols and false objects of worship you serve. **"So take a straight path to Him"** (*fastaqīmū ilayhi*) — worship Him alone sincerely, in accordance with what He has commanded through His Messengers. **"And seek His forgiveness"** — for your past sins. **"And woe to the polytheists"** — doom and destruction is their lot.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān sums up what was still open to them even now: turn in worship and obedience to Allah alone, repent, and renounce past sins.

## "Those who do not give the zakāh" (ayah 7)

Ayah 7 describes the mushrikīn as those who do not give the zakāh and who disbelieve in the Hereafter — which raises questions the commentators take seriously.

**What zakāh means here.** ʿAlī ibn Abī Ṭalḥah reported from Ibn ʿAbbās that it means those who do not bear witness that there is no god except Allah; ʿIkrimah held the same. Ibn Kathir supports this from the Qur'an's own use of the root — "indeed he succeeds who purifies himself (*zakkāhā*), and indeed he fails who corrupts himself" (91:9–10), and similarly 87:14–15 and 79:18. On this reading the zakāh meant is **purification of the soul** — ridding oneself of all bad qualities, the worst of which is shirk. Ibn Kathir adds a fine note in passing: the zakāh paid on wealth is so called precisely *because* it purifies wealth, and is a means of increasing and blessing it.

**The other view.** Qatādah said plainly: "They withheld the zakāh of their wealth." Ibn Kathir reports this as the apparent meaning according to many scholars of tafsīr, and the view Ibn Jarīr favoured. Both readings are transmitted; treat them as two attributed opinions.

**The chronological problem.** If zakāh is meant literally, how can Makkans be blamed for not paying it, when the obligation was instituted in the second year after the Hijrah while this āyah was revealed in Makkah? Ibn Kathir's answer: it is not unlikely that the principle of charity and zakāh was already in place, enjoined at the very beginning of the mission — as in "but pay the due thereof on the day of their harvest" (6:141) — while what was settled in Madīnah was the *detail*: how the amount is to be calculated according to the *nuṣub*. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān reports the same from him, adding that zakāh was obligated in principle along with ṣalāh from the beginning of Islam, as mentioned in Sūrah al-Muzzammil, and that what was fixed in Madīnah was the determination of the *niṣāb* — which Maʿārif ul Qurʼān glosses as the minimum capital and property at which zakāh becomes applicable — along with the arrangements for collecting it. So it is not correct to say zakāh carried no obligation in Makkah. Ibn Kathir gives a parallel: prayer too was first enjoined before sunrise and before sunset, and only on the Night of the Isrāʼ, a year and a half before the Hijrah, were the five daily prayers enjoined — their conditions explained later, in stages.

**Are non-Muslims addressed by the practical rulings?** A second question in Maʿārif ul Qurʼān: many jurists hold that non-Muslims are not addressed by the practical injunctions — ṣalāh, fasting, ḥajj, zakāh — until they first embrace faith. Why then this reproach? Many leading scholars of jurisprudence *do* hold that non-Muslims are addressed by the obligatory duties, and on that view there is no difficulty. Those holding the other position can say the real denunciation is not the non-payment itself but that it springs from disbelief and is a mark of it: had they believed, they would have been strict in paying, so their fault is their failure to embrace faith. (*Bayān ul-Qurʼān*.)

**Why zakāh and not ṣalāh?** A third question: ṣalāh is the weightiest commandment, so why single out zakāh? Maʿārif ul Qurʼān reports from Qurṭubī and others that the Quraysh were wealthy people known for giving alms and helping the poor — but when someone became a Muslim, they would cut him off from that help. Zakāh is named in order to denounce *that*. Allah knows best.

## A reward that is never cut off (ayah 8)

After the warning, the passage closes with a promise: those who believe and do righteous deeds have *ajrun ghayru mamnūn*. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān explains the key word: *mamnūn* here means something interrupted — so the reward of those firm in faith and regular in good deeds is continuous and unending. Ibn Kathir reports that Mujāhid and others said it will never be cut off or decrease, comparing "they shall abide therein for ever" (18:3) and "a gift without an end" (11:108).

There is a further, tender reading. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān notes that some exegetes explain the āyah to mean that if a Muslim regular in his religious duties is at some point unable to perform them — through illness, travel, or some other reason — the reward for those deeds is not cut off. Rather, Allah orders the angels to keep crediting to his account the good deeds he used to do in normal conditions but cannot do now. Aḥādīth on this subject are narrated in *Ṣaḥīḥ* of Bukhārī as reported by Sayyidnā Abū Mūsā al-Ashʿarī, in *Sharḥ us-Sunnah* of Baghawī by Sayyidnā Ibn ʿUmar and by Sayyidnā Anas, and in *Razīn* by Sayyidnā ʿAbdullāh ibn Masʿūd. (*Mazharī*)

## Living it

**Do not blame the Book** — ayah 3 forecloses that excuse; where understanding is missing, look first at the intention behind the reading. **Watch the excuse of helplessness**: "my heart isn't in it", "there's a wall between me and this" — ayah 5 puts such words in the mouths of people the Qur'an denounces, and the veil, say the commentators, descends only after refusal and lifts if the mind changes. **Answer contempt with humility**, as ayah 6 does: *I am only a man like you; so straighten toward Him and seek His forgiveness.*

passages.title: How can you disbelieve in the One who created?
passages.tafsir:
These four ayat are a single argument: the Creator of the earth, its mountains, its food supply and the seven heavens above it is the only Lord there is — so how can anyone deny Him, and place rivals beside Him? Ibn Kathir opens his comment simply: here Allah denounces the idolaters who worship other gods apart from Him, although He is the Creator, Subduer and Controller of all things. Ayah 9 puts the question. Ayat 10–12 are the evidence, a tour of the making of the universe — ending where ayah 9 began, with the majesty of the One being denied.

## The charge in ayah 9

The Prophet ﷺ is told to *say* it — the argument is put in his mouth as a challenge: "Do you verily disbelieve in Him Who created the earth in two Days? And you set up rivals with Him?" Those rivals, Ibn Kathir explains, are "false gods whom you worship alongside Him" — set up beside the One who made the ground you are standing on.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān states the purpose of the passage in the same terms: with reference to the greatness of the heavens and the earth and the wisdom underlying their creation, the mushriks (those who associate partners with Allah) are reprimanded for a belief that is simply irrational — that a Creator of this power should need partners to carry out His divine functions. Maʿārif points to the same rebuke in Sūrat al-Baqarah: "How is it that you deny Allah despite that you were lifeless and He gave you life…? It is He who created for you all that the earth contains; then He turned to the heavens and made them seven skies" (2:28–29). The difference, Maʿārif notes, is that al-Baqarah gives no order of creation and no number of days; Sūrah Fuṣṣilat is where those details are supplied.

The closing phrase of ayah 9 — "That is the Lord of all that exists" — is, in Ibn Kathir's words, the plain conclusion: the Creator of all things is the Lord of all the creatures. Creation and lordship are not two claims; they are one.

## Earth first, then the roof

Ibn Kathir observes that this passage is the detailed explanation of a summary given elsewhere: "Who created the heavens and the earth in Six Days" (7:54). Here the two are discussed separately, with their days counted out. And Allah mentions the earth first, Ibn Kathir says, "because it is the foundation, and the foundation should be built first, then the roof."

## The question that troubled a man — and Ibn ʿAbbās's answer

In Sūrat an-Nāziʿāt Allah mentions building the heaven — raising it, perfecting it, covering its night with darkness, bringing out its forenoon — then says, "And after that He spread the earth, And brought forth therefrom its water and its pasture. And the mountains He has fixed firmly" (79:27–33). So which came first? Ibn Kathir's summary of the difficulty: this ayah states that the *spreading out* of the earth came after the creation of the heavens, but the earth itself was created before the heavens according to some texts.

Ibn Kathir records that this difficulty was brought to Ibn ʿAbbās (may Allah be pleased with him), in a narration from Saʿīd bin Jubayr that **al-Bukhārī** recorded in his *Ṣaḥīḥ*, in his Tafsir of this very ayah. A man came listing things in the Qur'an that confused him: that there will be "no kinship among them that Day, nor will they ask of one another" (23:101) yet also "they will turn to one another and question one another" (37:27); that they "will never be able to hide a single fact from Allah" (4:42) yet will say, "By Allah, our Lord, we were not those who joined others in worship with Allah" (6:23); that heaven is mentioned before earth in 79:27–30 but earth before heaven here; and that Allah says He *was* Oft-Forgiving, Most Merciful (4:96), Most Powerful, All-Wise (4:56), All-Hearer, All-Seer (4:58) — "it is as if He was and is no longer."

Ibn ʿAbbās answered each in turn. The silence and the questioning belong to different moments of that Day: at the first blowing of the Trumpet all in the heavens and the earth swoon away (39:68), and then there is no kinship and no asking; when the Horn is blown again, they turn to one another and question one another. The idolaters' denial of shirk is a lie they attempt when Allah forgives the sincere believers their sins — until a seal is placed over their mouths and their hands speak, and it is known that not a single fact can be hidden from Allah.

Then the creation. Ibn ʿAbbās said: Allah created the earth in two days, then He created the heavens, then He turned to the heaven and gave it its shape in two more days. Then He *spread* the earth — and spreading it means that He brought forth from it its water and its pasture, and created the mountains, sands, inanimate things, rocks and hills and everything in between, in two more days. That is what "He spread the earth" (79:30) refers to. So He created the earth and everything in it in four days, and He created the heavens in two.

And on the word *kāna* — "He **was** Oft-Forgiving, Most Merciful" — Ibn ʿAbbās said: this is how He described Himself, and this is how He still is. Whatever Allah wills comes to pass. His closing counsel: **"so do not be confused about the Qur'an, for all of it comes from Allah."**

## Two ways the scholars fit the days together

Ibn Kathir maps the six days onto named days: the earth in two days means Sunday and Monday; the blessing of the earth and the measuring out of its sustenance was Tuesday and Wednesday, "which together with the two previous days add up to four days"; and the seven heavens were finished in two more days, Thursday and Friday. Named that way, the earth's four days run continuously.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān records a related but different resolution from Maulānā Ashraf ʿAlī Thānawī in *Bayān-ul-Qurʼān*. Thānawī notes that although the creation of the earth and the skies is mentioned briefly or in detail in hundreds of places in the Qur'an, its *sequence* is probably mentioned in only three verses: this passage, the verses of al-Baqarah above, and 79:27–32. He concluded that only the **matter** of the earth came into existence first; before it was moulded into shape, the matter of the sky came into existence in the form of smoke; after that the earth was moulded into shape with its mountains and trees; and then the seven skies were given form out of that floating smoky matter. He offers this as the harmony between the verses, and closes: **only Allah knows the truth.** Maʿārif adds that Ibn ʿAbbās's explanation reported in the *Ṣaḥīḥ* of al-Bukhārī comes to about the same thing.

Summarising, Maʿārif says the four days of the earth's creation were probably **not continuous**: two days for the earth and the matter of the mountains, then two days for the skies, then two final days in which the laying out of the earth — mountains, trees, rivers, springs — was completed. And Allah knows best.

**One point that is not in dispute.** Maʿārif states that by the consensus of the exegetes, the four days of ayah 10 *include* the two days of ayah 9. They are not additional. Otherwise the total period of creation would come to eight days, which is against the explicit statement of the Qur'an: "And We created the heavens and the earth and all that is between them in six days, and no weariness even touched Us" (50:38).

## A lesson in how to weigh reports

Ibn Kathir relates, with reference to Ibn Jarīr, a narration in which the Jews of Madinah came to the Prophet ﷺ and asked about the creation of the earth and the skies, and were told: the earth on Sunday and Monday, the mountains and the minerals in it on Tuesday, and the trees, water springs, cities, buildings and desolate plains on Wednesday — four days, as the ayah says; then the sky on Thursday; and on Friday the stars, the sun, the moon and the angels, with the creation of Sayyidnā Ādam (peace be upon him) in the last hours. Ibn Kathir comments that **this hadith has an element of *gharābah*** — its contents are not corroborated by other sources. Maʿārif adds a reason: it places the creation of Ādam (peace be upon him), the command to prostrate and Iblīs's expulsion from Paradise all in that same final hour, whereas it is patently clear from the text of many verses of the Qur'an that Ādam's creation came a long time after the earth and skies were made and provisioned (Maẓharī).

There is also a hadith narrated by Sayyidnā Abū Hurayrah (may Allah be pleased with him), reported in the *Ṣaḥīḥ* of Muslim, according to which creation commenced on Saturday and took seven days. Because the explicit verses of the Qur'an give the duration as six days, and because of its chain of narrators, Maʿārif reports that the leading muḥaddithīn have held this hadith *maʿlūl* — defective. Ibn Kathir stated that it is one of the strange narrations of the *Ṣaḥīḥ* of Muslim, and that Imām al-Bukhārī in his *Tārīkh Kabīr* considered it defective; some scholars have quoted it as a saying of Abū Hurayrah narrated from Kaʿb al-Aḥbār rather than a statement of the Prophet ﷺ, and have said that this is the most correct. Other masters of hadith — Ibn al-Madīnī, al-Bayhaqī and others — likewise considered it a statement of Kaʿb al-Aḥbār.

Maʿārif's conclusion: of all the ahadith narrating the duration, days and sequence of creation, none can be said to be as absolutely certain as the Qur'an, and it is very likely that some of these are Israelite traditions rather than noble ahadith. **Therefore conclusions should be drawn from the verses of the Qur'an only.** What is found absolutely certain from the Qur'an collectively is that the earth, the skies and whatever is inside them were created in six days; that the earth with its mountains and trees took a full four days; and the skies two — though Maʿārif notes the verses do not make clear whether both were full days.

## Ayah 10: a furnished house

**"He placed therein firm mountains from above it."** Maʿārif notes that the Qur'an clarifies in many verses that the mountains were created to maintain the earth's balance, and that this purpose alone did not require them to be raised above the earth's surface and made so high; they could have been placed inside the earth. But in raising them high — generally beyond the reach of human beings and animals — there are thousands, rather innumerable, benefits for the inhabitants of the earth, and the words "**from above it**" point to precisely that special blessing.

**"And He blessed it."** Ibn Kathir: He blessed it and gave it the potential to be planted with seeds and to bring forth produce.

**"And measured therein its sustenance."** *Aqwāt* is the plural of *qūt*, which, as Abū ʿUbayd is cited, means food and sustenance, including the common necessities of human life. Ibn Kathir explains the phrase as what the earth's people need of provision, and places in which to plant things and grow crops. But the beauty is in what the early scholars saw in the measuring out: ʿIkrimah and Mujāhid said, "He placed in every land that which is not suited for any other land." Ḥasan and Suddī said Allah has predetermined the sustenance and maintenance of the inhabitants of every region according to their need — which is why every region has characteristics of its own, and different kinds of minerals, vegetation, trees and animals.

Maʿārif draws this out with real delight: different regions yield different products and different dress — ʿaṣb in Yemen, Sābūrī in Sābūr, ṭayālisah in Ray; wheat in one region, rice and other grains elsewhere; cotton in some areas, jute in others; apples and grapes in some places, mangoes in others. And then the point: **ʿIkrimah and Ḍaḥḥāk state that these very differences have opened the way for international trade and for mutual cooperation between the regions and countries of the world.** No region is independent of the others for the fulfilment of its needs; mutual want is the only firm basis for mutual cooperation. ʿIkrimah has stated that in some areas salt is sold for an equal weight of gold.

Maʿārif sums it up: Allah has made this earth a great store of all the necessities — food, shelter, clothing — of all its inhabitants, the billions of humans and innumerable animals to come into this world up to the Last Day; these have been kept inside it and will keep growing and being supplied as needed; all a person has to do is take out what he needs.

**"Equal for all those who ask."** Two readings are reported, and both are good:

- Most of the commentators relate this to the four days: all this great creation took place in *exactly* four days. Maʿārif notes that "four" in ordinary speech does not always mean exactly four — it may be slightly more or less, with the fractions disregarded; the word "equal" rules that out. And "those who ask" means the people who asked the Prophet ﷺ about the creation of the earth and the skies, as the Jews did according to *Tafsīr Ibn Jarīr* and *ad-Durr-ul-Manthūr* (Ibn Kathir, Qurṭubī, Rūḥ). Ibn ʿAbbās, Qatādah and as-Suddī likewise read it as "for whoever wants to ask about that" — Ibn Kathir adds, so that they might know.
- Ibn Zayd and some other exegetes link the words instead to the measuring of sustenance: "those who ask" are the needy, since needy people usually ask for food. On this reading, Allah has created these kinds of provision for the benefit of those who need and seek them, and measures out for each person what he is in need of (*al-Baḥr al-Muḥīṭ*). Ibn Kathir quotes this explanation and says it is like "And He gave you of all that you asked for" (14:34) — where "asked for" means "were in need of", even where nothing was asked literally, since Allah bestows even on those who did not ask.

## Ayah 11: the smoke that answered

**"Then He rose over (istawā ilā) the heaven when it was smoke"** — Ibn Kathir explains the smoke as steam which arose from the earth when the earth was created.

Then the command: **"Come both of you, willingly or unwillingly."** Ibn Kathir renders the sense as: respond to My command and be subjected to this action, willingly or unwillingly. And the answer: **"We come willingly"** — meaning, Ibn Kathir says, we will respond to You willingly, and everything that You want to create in us — angels, jinn and men — will all be obedient to You.

Notice where that leaves the people addressed in ayah 9. The sky, still formless smoke, and the earth answer their Lord with instant, glad obedience; the human being, made and fed by Him, sets up rivals beside Him.

**Was the exchange literal?** Maʿārif reports a genuine difference. According to some exegetes, the command and the compliant reply are a metaphorical expression for the readiness of the earth and the sky to comply with every order from Allah. But Ibn ʿAṭiyyah and other leading research scholars have stated that this is no metaphor — it is based on reality: Allah had endowed the earth and the skies with the faculty of intellect and comprehension of the commands addressed to them, and with the power of speaking and replying. *Tafsīr al-Baḥr al-Muḥīṭ*, after quoting this explanation, held it to be the most suitable and the best. Ibn Kathir, after quoting it, also quotes the statement of some exegetes that the earth's reply was given by that portion of the earth on which the Baytullāh has been constructed, and the sky's reply by that portion of the sky just above it, known as al-Bayt al-Maʿmūr.

## Ayah 12: seven heavens, and lamps that guard

**"Then He completed and finished their creation as seven heavens in two Days"** — He finished forming them as seven heavens in two more days, Ibn Kathir says, which were Thursday and Friday. **"And He decreed in each heaven its affair"**: He placed in each heaven whatever it needs of angels, and things which are known only to Him.

**"And We adorned the nearest heaven with lamps"** — the stars and planets, Ibn Kathir says, which shine on the people of the earth. **"As well as to guard"**: as protection against the shayāṭīn, lest they listen to the angels on high. What a person sees as decoration is, from another angle, a fortification.

The passage closes with **"Such is the decree of Him, the Almighty, the All-Knower."** Ibn Kathir: the Almighty Who has subjugated all things to His control, the All-Knower Who knows all the movements of His creatures. These are exactly the two Names the argument needs — the Almighty, so that no rival can be imagined beside Him; the All-Knower, so that nothing here is accident.

## Living with these ayat

**Let creation argue for you.** The passage begins not with abstractions but with ground, mountains, food, stars — the ordinary furniture of a life — and asks the listener to trace it back to its Owner. Look at what is on your plate, or at the sky at night, and let it finish the sentence.

**Receive provision as measured, not random.** *And measured therein its sustenance.* The salt in one land and the gold in another are a distribution — and one that, as ʿIkrimah and Ḍaḥḥāk saw, makes peoples need each other.

**Do not let a difficulty in the Qur'an unsettle you.** A man came to Ibn ʿAbbās with the things that confused him, and was answered plainly and sent away with the words: do not be confused about the Qur'an, for all of it comes from Allah. Ask — and ask someone who knows.

**Answer as they answered.** Heaven and earth said, *"We come willingly."* The whole passage is asking one question of the reader: and you?

passages.title: The thunderbolt of 'Ad and Thamud
passages.tafsir:
These six ayat form one continuous warning shaped as history. The Prophet ﷺ is told what to say if the people he is addressing finally turn their backs, and the answer is not a new argument but a memory: two great nations, 'Ad and Thamud, who heard the same call and refused it, and what became of them. From ayah 13 to ayah 18 a single sentence is stretched across the passage — *if you turn away, this is what turning away has cost before* — and it does not resolve until the very last line, where a handful of people are carried out of the ruin alive.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān states the purpose plainly. These verses warn the people of Makkah that if, even after seeing the manifest proofs of the Oneness of Allah, they do not accept the call of the Holy Prophet ﷺ, they may face a punishment like that which the earlier peoples of 'Ad and Thamud faced. A brief account of what happened to those peoples is then given. And the people of Makkah are reminded that their punishment on the Day of Judgment will be much more severe, and that they will not be able to escape it — because even the organs of their own bodies will testify against them.

So the history is not told for its own sake. It is told as a mirror.

## The word that opens the passage: *ṣāʿiqah*

Ibn Kathir paraphrases the command of ayah 13: *Say, O Muhammad, to these idolators who disbelieve in the message of truth that you have brought — if you turn away from that which I have brought to you from Allah, then I warn you of the punishment of Allah like the punishment that the past nations suffered for disbelieving in the Messengers.* And he immediately widens the frame: 'Ad and Thamud are named as examples, not as a closed list. The same fate met "other similar nations who did what they did."

The key word is **ṣāʿiqah**. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān, citing Qurtubi, explains that it originally means *something that renders a person unconscious*. From that core sense two familiar uses branch out: a thunderbolt is called a ṣāʿiqah, and so is any unforeseen calamity or disaster. Both senses live inside this passage, and the passage will go on to show them working out in two different ways on two different peoples.

Notice how exact the warning is: *a ṣāʿiqah like the ṣāʿiqah of 'Ad and Thamud*. Not "some punishment" but *that* one — a blow that arrives before you can brace for it and leaves you insensible.

## They were never short of evidence

Ayah 14 answers the objection nobody has yet raised: *but were they warned?*

The phrase *min bayni aydīhim wa min khalfihim* — "from before them and behind them" — is opened up by Ibn Kathir with a parallel verse about Hud, the brother of 'Ad, who warned his people in al-Ahqaf: *"And surely, there have passed away warners before him and after him"* (46:21). The meaning, Ibn Kathir says, is that in the neighbouring towns and cities Allah sent Messengers who commanded the people to worship Allah alone with no partner or associate, and who brought good news as well as warnings.

Then he presses further, and this is the heart of the ayah: **they saw the punishment Allah sent upon His enemies, and the blessings He bestowed upon His friends** — and despite all of this they did not believe. On the contrary, they denied and rejected the Messengers. The evidence reached them from every direction, in time and in place, from earlier warners and later ones, from the town next door and from their own brother among them. What they lacked was never information.

**Their excuse.** They answered with an argument that sounds sophisticated and is really an evasion: *"If our Lord had so willed, He would surely have sent down the angels."* Ibn Kathir explains the claim — meaning, if Allah were to send Messengers, they would be angels sent from His presence. And then the sting in the tail: *"So, indeed we disbelieve in that with which you have been sent"* — which Ibn Kathir renders as, *because you are a mere human; we will not follow you because you are just men like us.*

Strip away the wrapping and the objection is pride. They were not asking a question about angels; they were refusing to be corrected by someone who eats and sleeps as they do. Every generation has its version of this — an insistence that guidance, to be worth accepting, must arrive in a form that costs the hearer no humility.

## Two nations, two ways of refusing

From ayah 15 the passage divides into a pair, and the pairing is the point. *As for 'Ad…* and then, in ayah 17, *as for Thamud…* — two case studies, deliberately set side by side, each with its own disease.

**'Ad refused out of strength.** Ibn Kathir glosses *they were arrogant in the land without right* as: they were arrogant, stubborn and disobedient. Their slogan, *"Who is mightier than us in strength?"*, was a boast about physical strength and power — and, Ibn Kathir adds, **they thought that this would protect them from Allah's punishment**. That is the whole delusion in one line: they treated their own muscle as a shield against the One who gave them the muscle. The Qur'an's reply in the same ayah is devastatingly simple: *See they not that Allah Who created them was mightier in strength than them?* Ibn Kathir unfolds it — do they not realise, even as they show open enmity, that He is the Almighty who created all things and **gave them whatever strength they have**, and that His onslaught will be far greater? He cites alongside it the verse *"With Hands did We construct the heaven. Verily, We are able to extend the vastness of space thereof"* (51:47). They openly opposed the Almighty, Ibn Kathir says, denied His signs and disobeyed His Messenger. Ayah 15 closes by naming the deeper crime: *they used to deny Our signs*. The strength was the boast; the denial was the sin.

**Thamud refused out of preference.** Their failure is subtler and, in a way, more frightening: *We showed them the path of truth, but they preferred blindness to guidance.* On *fa-hadaynāhum*, "We showed them the path of truth," Ibn Kathir reports the early authorities: **Ibn 'Abbas (may Allah be pleased with him), Abu al-'Aliyah, Sa'id ibn Jubayr, Qatadah, as-Suddi and Ibn Zayd** all said it means "We explained to them," while **ath-Thawri** said "We called them." Either reading gives guidance *offered and made plain* — the truth set before them clearly, the invitation extended. And so the verdict lands with a verb of choice: they **preferred** blindness. Not "they missed it," not "it never reached them." Ibn Kathir spells out the history behind that word: Allah showed them the truth and made it clear to them through the words of their Prophet Salih, but they opposed him and rejected him, and they slaughtered the she-camel of Allah, which He had made a sign for them of the truth of their Prophet.

Set the two together and you have two whole grammars of refusal. One says *we are too strong to need this.* The other says *we have seen it, and we would rather not.* The passage does not rank them. It simply shows that both end in the same place.

## Two punishments, one disgrace

Each nation is answered in a way that fits its refusal, and the sources are careful to keep the two events distinct.

For 'Ad it was wind. *So We sent upon them a ṣarṣar wind in days of calamity.* Ibn Kathir records three explanations of **ṣarṣar** among the scholars: some said a strongly blowing wind; others, a cold wind; others still, the wind that makes a noise. His own conclusion is that it was all of these at once, and he shows why each fits — it was a strong wind, an apt punishment for a people deceived by their physical strength; it was intensely cold, as in *"with a ṣarṣar wind"* (69:6), which he says means a very cold wind; and it made a furious sound, so much so that he mentions a famous river in the east called Ṣarṣar precisely because of the noise it makes as it flows. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān, citing Qurtubi, describes the same event as a wild tempest of extremely high speed with a piercing sound, and notes that this storm was itself a ṣāʿiqah — the calamity named back in ayah 13. Feel the reversal: they asked *who is mightier than us in strength?* and were answered by moving air.

For Thamud it was something else. Ibn Kathir says that *the ṣāʿiqah of disgracing torment seized them* means Allah sent upon them the Sayhah (the blast), the earthquake, and intense humiliation, punishment and torment. And *because of what they used to earn* means, he says, because of their disbelief and rejection. The word "earn" matters: nothing arbitrary happened to them. They were paid.

**"In days of calamity."** Ibn Kathir takes *ayyāmin naḥisāt* to mean consecutive days, linking it to *"seven nights and eight days in succession"* (69:7) and *"on a day of calamity, continuous"* (54:19): the punishment began on a day which was of evil omen for them, and that evil omen continued until, in his words, they were destroyed — every last one of them — and their humiliation in this world was joined to their punishment in the Hereafter. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān adds detail from the earlier authorities. Dahhak said that rain had been withheld from them by Allah for three years, with dry tempestuous winds blowing all the while, and then eight days and seven nights of continuous, extremely severe windstorm. Some narrations place the event at the end of the month of Shawwal, beginning on a Wednesday and running until the following Wednesday, and add that whenever a nation has been subjected to a scourge it has happened on a Wednesday (Qurtubi, Mazhari). Maʿārif ul Qurʼān also relates that Sayyidnā Jābir ibn ʿAbdullāh (may Allah be pleased with him) stated: when Allah Almighty wants the welfare of a nation, He orders rain to fall on them and stops the very fast winds from blowing over them; when a nation is to face misfortune, rain is withheld from them and strong winds begin to blow frequently.

**The word that binds both endings is disgrace.** Ayah 16 states the purpose: *that We might give them a taste of disgracing torment in this present worldly life* — and then, *the torment of the Hereafter will be more disgracing*, which Ibn Kathir glosses as more humiliating still. And *they will never be helped*: Ibn Kathir explains that in the Hereafter they will find no help, just as they were never helped in this world, and they had no one who could protect them from Allah or save them from His punishment. Ayah 17 uses the same note for Thamud — *the ṣāʿiqah of disgracing torment*. A people obsessed with standing were brought low, and the lowering is not finished yet.

## The unlucky days that were not unlucky in themselves

That Wednesday narration could easily be misread, and Maʿārif ul Qurʼān blocks the misreading immediately. This is one of the most practically important notes in the whole passage, and it sits right in the middle of it.

It is established by the principles of Islam and by the ahadith of the Holy Prophet ﷺ that **no day or night is in itself unlucky or ill-omened**. The days of the windstorm over the people of 'Ad have been called "unlucky" because those days had become ill-omened *for them*, on account of their own misdeeds. It does not necessarily mean that those days were ill-omened for everybody (Mazhari, Bayān ul-Qur'ān).

This is worth carrying home. The Qur'an names days of calamity and then, almost in the same breath, refuses to let you turn them into superstition. What made those days black was not the days. It was what the people had earned in them.

## And We saved those who believed

The passage does not end in ruin. Its last line is a rescue: *And We saved those who believed and had taqwa* — taqwa being that watchful mindfulness of Allah that keeps a person careful about what Allah has commanded and forbidden.

Ibn Kathir's comment is quietly beautiful. It means, he says, *We saved them from among them, and no harm came to them* — Allah saved them along with His Prophet Salih (peace be upon him), **because of their fear of Allah**. Read that against everything that came before. In a town that had earned annihilation, in the middle of a passage full of thunderbolts and freezing wind and earthquake, faith and fear of Allah carved out an exemption. Those people were not saved because they were many, or mighty, or because they could answer 'Ad's question — *who is mightier than us in strength?* They were saved because they believed, and because they feared Allah.

That is where the six ayat have been heading all along. The warning of ayah 13 and the rescue of ayah 18 are two halves of one offer.

## What this passage asks of us

**Do not treat capacity as security.** 'Ad's error was not having strength; it was assuming strength answers to nobody. Ibn Kathir's phrase should stay with us — Allah *gave them whatever strength they have*. Everything we might boast of was handed to us by the One we would be boasting against.

**Do not mistake clarity for guidance.** Thamud had the explanation, the Prophet, the miraculous sign — and preferred blindness. Knowing what is right is not the same as choosing it. The passage's opening word is *aʿraḍū*, "they turned away," and it is aimed at exactly the person who has understood the reminder and turns from it anyway.

**Refuse superstition.** No day and no night carries misfortune in its own nature. What makes a day black is what a person earns in it.

**And take the ending seriously.** The last word of the passage is not the storm but the deliverance. The same Power that let loose the ṣarṣar wind kept the believers untouched inside it. The door the passage leaves open is exactly the one ayah 18 names — īmān and taqwa, belief and mindfulness of Allah — and it is still open.

passages.title: Limbs testify against their owners
passages.tafsir:
This passage takes us to the edge of the Fire and lets us listen in on a conversation no one imagines having: a person arguing with his own body. Ayat 19–25 form one continuous scene — the gathering, the testimony, the recrimination, the diagnosis of what really destroyed these people, and finally a look back at how they were led there in the first place.

What holds the unit together is a single idea pursued to its end: **the sin you thought was private was never private.** The instruments you sinned with are the witnesses that will convict you, and the reason you sinned so freely was a false thought you were carrying about Allah Himself.

## Ayah 19 — Marched to the Fire in ranks

"And the Day the enemies of Allah are gathered to the Fire, and they are held in ranks."

Ibn Kathir explains that this is addressed to the idolaters as a reminder: remember the Day you will be gathered to the Fire and driven, when the keepers of Hell will gather the first of them with the last of them. He connects it to Allah's words elsewhere, *"And We shall drive the criminals to Hell, in a thirsty state"* (19:86).

The word the ayah turns on is **yūzaʿūn**. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān notes it comes from *wazʿ*, which means "to stop" or "to prevent." Most of the exegetes, it says, understood it this way: the people of Hell will be so numerous that as they are taken toward the plain of gathering and the place of reckoning, those at the front are halted for a while so that those at the back can catch up — so that there is no disorder. Other exegetes, Maʿārif adds citing Qurtubi, read *yūzaʿūn* as "pushed," meaning they are driven forward toward the reckoning.

Either way the picture is the same, and it is deliberately unflattering. These are not people walking; they are a crowd being managed. The very first thing the passage takes from them is what they prized most in this world — the sense of being in charge of themselves.

## Ayah 20 — The witnesses are already inside you

"Until, when they reach it, their hearing and their eyes and their skins testify against them as to what they used to do."

Ibn Kathir says *"when they reach it"* means when they stand at its very edge — at the brink, before entry. And the scope of the testimony is total: it covers **all their deeds, earlier and later; not a single letter will be concealed.**

Notice who the witnesses are. Not strangers. Not a neighbour who saw something through a window. The case is built entirely out of the accused. Hearing, sight, skin — these were the very tools of the sin, and now they are the record of it.

Not a single letter. That phrase is worth sitting with before moving on. We tend to picture the reckoning as a summary — the broad shape of a life, the headline items. Ibn Kathir's expression leaves no room for that comfort. The record is complete because the recorder was never external to us in the first place.

## Ayah 21 — "Why did you testify against us?"

"And they will say to their skins, 'Why did you testify against us?' They will say: 'Allah caused us to speak, who caused all things to speak; and He created you the first time, and to Him you are returned.'"

Ibn Kathir describes this exactly as it reads: they will blame their limbs and their skins for testifying against them, and the limbs will answer. There is something painfully human in the reflex — even at the lip of the Fire, the first instinct is to look for someone to blame, and the only party left to blame is oneself.

The skins' answer is a small sermon in theology. *Allah caused us to speak — the One who causes all things to speak.* Speech in a skin is no stranger than speech on a tongue; both are Allah's doing. And they add the argument that settles it: *He created you the first time.* Ibn Kathir glosses this to mean that Allah cannot be opposed or resisted, and to Him you will return. The One who brought speech out of nothing when He first made you can bring speech out of your skin today. Denying the second is only possible if you had already forgotten the first.

## From the Sunnah — the smile of the Prophet ﷺ

Ibn Kathir records, through Al-Hafiz Abu Bakr Al-Bazzar from Anas ibn Malik (may Allah be pleased with him), that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ laughed and smiled one day and said, *"Will you not ask me why I laughed?"* They said, "O Messenger of Allah, why did you laugh?" He said that he was amazed at how a servant will dispute with his Lord on the Day of Resurrection.

The servant will say, "My Lord, did You not promise me that You would not treat me unjustly?" Allah will say, "Yes." The man will say, "Then I will not accept any witness against me except from myself." Allah will say, "Is it not sufficient that I and the angels, the noble scribes, are witnesses?" These words are repeated several times — then a seal is placed over his mouth, and his limbs speak about what he used to do. Then he says to them: **"Away with you! It was only for your sake that I was arguing!"**

Ibn Kathir notes this was recorded by Al-Bazzar and by Ibn Abi Hatim, and also by Muslim and An-Nasa'i. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān reports the same hadith from Anas as narrated in Sahih Muslim, with a few extra strokes: the man asks that some part of his own being stand as witness, and Allah answers him with His own words, *"Sufficient is your own self this Day as a reckoner against you"* (17:14). Then the seal is placed, the organs are asked, and every organ speaks the truth. Afterwards his mouth is unsealed and he says to his own organs in displeasure: may you be ruined and destroyed — *everything I did in the world, I did to keep you comfortable.*

Sit with why the Prophet ﷺ laughed. It is not cruelty; it is astonishment at a creature arguing with his Creator — and at the exquisite justice of the answer. The man demanded that nothing but his own self be allowed to convict him. He was granted exactly that. He got the terms he asked for.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān adds a narration from Abu Hurairah (may Allah be pleased with him) that this person's mouth will be sealed and his thigh will be called to speak, and his thigh — its flesh and its bone — will testify to his deeds (Muslim, Mazhari). Ibn Kathir records from Ibn Abi Hatim, from Abu Burdah from Abu Musa, that the disbeliever or the hypocrite will be shown his deeds and will deny them, swearing by Allah's glory that the angel wrote down something he never did; the angel will name the day and the place, and still he will swear he did not do it — and at that point the seal is placed over his mouth. Al-Ashʿari (may Allah be pleased with him) said, "I think that the first part of his body to speak will be his right thigh."

## Ayah 22 — Three men under the Kaʿbah's cloth

This ayah has a story behind it, and the story unlocks it.

Ibn Kathir records from Imam Ahmad that ʿAbdullah (may Allah be pleased with him) said: "I was hiding beneath the covering of the Kaʿbah, and three men came along — a man from Quraysh and two of his brothers-in-law from Thaqif, or a man from Thaqif and two of his brothers-in-law from Quraysh. Their bellies were very fat, and they did not have much understanding. They said some words I could not hear, then one of them said, 'Do you think Allah can hear what we are saying now?' The other said, 'If we raise our voices He will hear it, but if we do not raise our voices He will not hear it.' The other said, 'If He can hear one thing from us, He can hear everything.'"

He mentioned this to the Prophet ﷺ, and Allah revealed: *"And you were not concealing yourselves lest your hearing and your eyes and your skins testify against you — but you assumed that Allah does not know much of what you do"* — through to *"of those utterly lost."* Ibn Kathir says this is how At-Tirmidhi recorded it, that a similar report came through Ahmad by a different chain and through Muslim and At-Tirmidhi, and that Al-Bukhari and Muslim also recorded it through another chain.

That overheard whisper is the whole disease in miniature. It is not a denial of Allah — it is a *shrinking* of Allah. What those men imagined was a lord who catches the loud parts and misses the quiet ones; they pictured for themselves a hearing with limits and edges to it, and then lived inside the space they thought that left them. The third man is the only one who reasons correctly, and his reasoning is simply this: hearing that is real is not partial.

So read ayah 22 with that in your ear. Ibn Kathir explains it as what the organs and skins say back to their owners when they are blamed: *you did not hide from us what you were doing — on the contrary, you openly committed disbelief and sin, and you claimed you did not care, because you did not believe that Allah knew about all your deeds.* The ayah is not saying "you tried to hide and failed." It is saying **you did not even bother to try**, because you had privately decided there was nothing to hide from.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān, commenting on this very ayah, draws the conclusion plainly: a person who wants to commit a sin or a crime can hide it from other people — but how is he to hide it from his own limbs and organs? "Our ears, eyes, hands, feet, skin and hair are not ours," it says; rather they are witnesses of our condition standing against us, and when they are questioned about our deeds they will give true evidence. Therefore there is no way at all to conceal a sin or a crime — and, in its words, **the only way to avoid that disgrace is to keep away from sin.** There is no strategy of concealment available. There is only the choice not to do it.

## Ayah 23 — The thought that killed them

"And that assumption of yours which you assumed about your Lord has ruined you, and you have become of the losers."

This is the verdict of the whole passage, and it names the murder weapon. Not an act. A **ẓann** — an assumption, a thought entertained about Allah.

Ibn Kathir: this evil thought — your belief that Allah did not know much of what you were doing — is what caused you to be doomed and made you losers before your Lord. And *"you have become of those utterly lost"* means that at the place of Resurrection you have lost your own selves and your families.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān traces the same causal chain and makes it sharper, and it presses the point as a plain appeal to reason. It concedes that people who denied Allah's oneness and denied prophethood would never have expected their own organs to speak up before Allah and give evidence against them — but says any intelligent person could have understood that it is utterly impossible that the One who created him from a lowly substance, gave him the ability to hear and see, brought him up and made him young, should not fully know his deeds and his condition. *But you thought, against everything that was evident, that Allah had no knowledge of many of your deeds* — and it was that false assumption that emboldened them into shirk and kufr. Maʿārif states explicitly that this is the meaning of ayah 23.

The bad theology came first. The bad life followed.

This is where the passage reaches into an ordinary believer's chest. Almost nobody says out loud that Allah does not see. But there is a version of that whisper under the Kaʿbah's cloth in every quiet compromise: the assumption, never stated, that this particular thing is beneath His notice. That is the *ẓann* the ayah is talking about, and the ayah says it is capable of ruining a person.

## Ayah 24 — Two doors, both shut

"So if they endure, the Fire is their home; and if they seek to make amends, they will not be of those allowed to make amends."

Ibn Kathir puts it starkly: whether they bear it patiently or not, they are in the Fire and will have no escape and no way out; and even if they try to please Allah and offer excuses, nothing of that will be accepted from them.

Ibn Jarir explains the second half — *"and if they seek to please Allah"* — as this: they will ask to be sent back to this world, and that plea will not be answered. He cited as its parallel, *"They will say: 'Our Lord, our wretchedness overcame us, and we were an erring people. Our Lord, bring us out of it; if we return, then indeed we would be wrongdoers.' He will say: 'Remain in it with ignominy, and speak not to Me'"* (23:106–108).

In this world we always have two options in trouble: endure it, or fix it. This ayah walks the reader to the Day when both doors are found bolted — and it tells us now, while the door for making amends is still open.

## Ayah 25 — Where it all began: the companions

"And We assigned to them companions who made attractive to them what was before them and what was behind them."

Having shown us the end, the passage turns back and shows the mechanism of the ruin. Ibn Kathir says that Allah here tells us that He is the One who sends the idolaters astray, that this happens by His will and decree, and that He is All-Wise in His actions — when He appoints for them close companions from among the devils of mankind and jinn.

That is a weighty statement, and it is received exactly as Allah revealed it, without adding to it and without explaining it away.

*"What was before them and what was behind them"* — Ibn Kathir explains that these companions made their past deeds look attractive to them, and as for the future, they see themselves as doing nothing but good. He cites the parallel: *"And whoever turns away blindly from the remembrance of the Most Gracious, We appoint for him a devil to be his companion. And indeed they hinder them from the path while they think that they are guided aright"* (43:36–37).

That is the most frightening note in the passage. These people were not miserable. Their past looked fine to them and their future looked fine to them, right up to the edge of the Fire. A feeling of reassurance is not evidence of being guided.

Then, *"and the Word was justified against them"* — Ibn Kathir: the Word of punishment, exactly as it had been justified against the nations of jinn and men who went before them and did what they did. And *"indeed they were losers"* means they are all equal in loss and ruin.

## Living it

The passage asks for one adjustment, and everything else follows from it.

**Correct your thought about Allah.** The chain in these ayat runs: a small assumption about what Allah does and does not notice → open sin without fear → a body that testifies → a Fire with no exit. The chain is broken at the first link and nowhere else.

**Treat your limbs as witnesses, not as property.** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān's formulation is worth carrying: your ears, eyes, hands, feet, skin and hair are not yours; they are witnesses of your condition standing against you, and they will give true evidence. And its conclusion is the only practical one — since concealment is impossible, the sole protection from that disgrace is to stay away from sin.

**Do not lose the day.** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān relates from Maʿqil ibn Yasar (may Allah be pleased with him) that the Prophet ﷺ said that every new day calls out to people: *I am a new day, and I will be a witness to whatever you do today; so do some good deed before I come to an end, so that I may testify for you — for once I am gone, you will never find me again* — and every night calls out the same. (Cited by Al-Qurtubi, with reference to Abu Nuʿaim.)

That is the mercy hidden inside a passage about the Fire. The witnesses are already assigned and already recording. Today they are still taking down testimony we would want read out.

passages.title: Their plan to shout the Quran down
passages.tafsir:
These four ayat follow one thing from beginning to end: a policy the disbelievers adopted towards the Qur'an, and what that policy finally costs them. Ayah 26 records the plan in their own words — drown the recitation out. Ayat 27 and 28 give Allah's answer to it. Ayah 29 lets us hear the same people speak again, much later, in the Fire — and what they say then is the opposite of the confident slogan they were shouting in ayah 26.

Notice the frame: ayah 26 opens **وَقَالَ الَّذِينَ كَفَرُوا** — "and those who disbelieve say" — and ayah 29 opens with the identical words. The same speakers, the same verb, two different worlds. In the first they are organising; in the second they are begging.

## The plan itself

Ibn Kathir explains ayah 26 in two layers. **لَا تَسْمَعُوا لِهَٰذَا الْقُرْآنِ** — "Listen not to this Qur'an" — means, in his words, that "they advised one another not to pay heed to the Qur'an or obey its commands." So the listening being forbidden is not merely sound reaching the ear; it is the listening that leads to heeding and obeying.

Then **وَالْغَوْا فِيهِ** — "and make noise in the midst of its (recitation)." Ibn Kathir reports this as the view of Mujahid: when it is recited, do not listen to it. And he explains the phrase further as "whistling and trying to make the Messenger of Allah ﷺ confused when he recited Qur'an, which is what the Quraysh did."

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān fills in the scene. It notes that this tactic came *after* other approaches had failed: "When all the efforts of the disbelievers failed in confronting the Holy Qur'an, they started doing such mischievous acts as mentioned in this verse." And it cites Sayyidnā Ibn ʿAbbās, may Allah be pleased with him, that **Abū Jahl got his people primed up and ready to make noises whenever Muhammad ﷺ recited the Qur'an, so that people might not find out what he was saying.** Others, Maʿārif adds, said that preparations were made to stop people from listening to the Qur'an "by whistling, clapping and by making all sorts of noises during the recitation."

Sit with that for a moment. This was not a stray heckle. It was prepared in advance — people primed and ready, waiting for the recitation to begin. And Ibn ʿAbbās names the purpose exactly: not to insult, not to argue, but *so that people might not find out what he was saying*. The words themselves had to be kept from reaching ears.

## What the plan tells us

Two details in the sources are worth holding together. Maʿārif says this came only after every other effort at confronting the Qur'an had failed — argument had been tried and had not worked. And Ibn ʿAbbās says the aim was to keep bystanders from making out the words. Whatever else it was, the noise was a substitute for a reply.

That is why the closing words of ayah 26 are so telling: **لَعَلَّكُمْ تَغْلِبُونَ** — "that you may overcome." Winning had been redefined. Not answering the Qur'an, not refuting it — just making sure nobody could hear it.

Ibn Kathir comments on this phrase that "this is the practice of these ignorant disbelievers **and those who follow in their footsteps**, when they hear the Qur'an." The behaviour is not sealed in Makkah. It is a pattern that recurs in anyone who cannot bear to let the Book get a hearing.

## Where such a mind comes from (the preceding ayah)

Ibn Kathir treats ayah 26 as continuous with what precedes it, and the connection is worth seeing. In ayah 25 Allah says He assigned to them intimate companions, "who have made fair seeming to them, what was before them and what was behind them." Ibn Kathir glosses: "they made their deeds attractive to them in the past. As far as the future is concerned, they only see themselves as doing good." He draws in the parallel from Sūrat al-Zukhruf: whoever turns away blindly from the remembrance of the Most Gracious, a Shaytan is appointed as a companion for him, "And verily, they hinder them from the path, but they think that they are guided aright!" (43:36–37).

That last clause is the psychology behind the whistling. In their own eyes these men were not villains disrupting revelation; they thought themselves guided. Evil that knows itself to be evil is easier to escape than evil that has been made to look attractive.

Ibn Kathir is careful here about the theology, and so should we be: "Allah tells us that He is the One Who sends the idolators astray, and that this happens with His will and decree. He is the All-Wise in His actions, when He appoints for them close companions from among the devils of man and jinn." Allah's decree encompasses everything, and He is All-Wise in all of it. And in the very same passage those same people are held accountable and punished for what *they* did. Ibn Kathir adds that "the Word is justified against them" means "the Word of torment, just as it was justified against the nations of the past who did what they did, men and Jinn alike," and that "Indeed they (all) were the losers" means "they are all equal in terms of loss and being doomed."

## The answer: ayat 27 and 28

Ayah 27 answers the slogan of ayah 26, and the translation carries the force of the Arabic in its two adverbs: "But **surely**, We shall cause those who disbelieve to taste a severe torment, and **certainly**, We shall requite them the worst of what they used to do." This is guarantee, not warning shot.

Ibn Kathir ties the punishment directly to the crime. "We shall cause those who disbelieve to taste a severe torment" means, he says, "in return for what they do when they hear the Qur'an." The very act described in ayah 26 is what is being answered. And "We shall requite them the worst of what they used to do" means, in his gloss, "for their evil deeds."

There is a bitter fitness in the word *taste*. They had refused the Qur'an entry through the ear; the torment will be given to them to taste — taken in and known from the inside, with no possibility of shutting it out.

Ayah 28 then names the recompense plainly: **ذَٰلِكَ جَزَاءُ أَعْدَاءِ اللَّهِ النَّارُ** — "That is the recompense of the enemies of Allah: the Fire." And **لَهُمْ فِيهَا دَارُ الْخُلْدِ** — "Therein will be for them the eternal home." That word *home* is chilling precisely because it is the language of belonging and settled rest. The stated cause comes at the end of the ayah: **جَزَاءً بِمَا كَانُوا بِآيَاتِنَا يَجْحَدُونَ** — "a recompense for that they used to deny Our Ayat." The noise was not an isolated bit of rudeness. It was denial made audible.

## Ayah 29: the cry from below

Now the same phrase returns — "And those who disbelieve will say" — but the tone has collapsed. **رَبَّنَا** — "Our Lord!" They address Him now. But look at what they ask for. Not forgiveness. Not release. They ask: **أَرِنَا اللَّذَيْنِ أَضَلَّانَا مِنَ الْجِنِّ وَالْإِنْسِ** — "Show us those among Jinn and men who led us astray, that we may crush them under our feet so that they become the lowest."

Even in the Fire, the instinct is to find someone to blame and someone to be beneath them.

Ibn Kathir explains the request concretely: "that we may crush them under our feet" means, "make them beneath us in the torment, so that they will be punished more severely than us"; and "so that they become the lowest" means "in the lowest level of Hell." He connects it with the scene in Sūrat al-Aʿrāf where the followers ask Allah to multiply the torment for their leaders, and Allah answers: **"For each one there is double (torment), but you know not"** (7:38) — which Ibn Kathir explains as: "Allah will give each of them the torment and punishment they deserve for their deeds." He cites as a further parallel that those who disbelieved and hindered others from the path of Allah will have "torment added to torment because they used to spread corruption" (16:88).

Put those two together as Ibn Kathir does. The misleaders genuinely do receive more — torment added to torment. But the measure for everyone is the same measure: what their own deeds deserve. The extra weight on the one who led you does not come off your own back.

**Who are "the two who led us astray"?** Ibn Kathir reports that it was said that ʿAlī, may Allah be pleased with him, said concerning this phrase: "Iblis and the son of Adam who killed his brother." And as-Suddi reported that ʿAlī, may Allah be pleased with him, explained the logic: "Iblis is followed by everyone who commits Shirk and the son of Adam is followed by everyone who commits a major sin. So Iblis is the one who calls people to every evil thing, such as Shirk and lesser sins."

The point is about *precedent*. Iblis opened the door of associating partners with Allah; the first murderer opened the door of the major sins committed by human hands. Every later sinner walks through a door someone else first pushed open — and the one who opened it carries a share.

Ibn Kathir supports this by citing a hadith about the first son of Adam. (The source before us does not name the collection it comes from, so it is quoted here without attributing it to any named collection.) Its meaning: **no soul is wrongfully killed but that a share of the burden of that sin falls upon the first son of Adam, because he was the first one who set the precedent of killing another.**

The flip side is sobering. Whoever sets a precedent — a habit, a mockery, a way of behaving that others copy — has a stake in everything that follows from it. Ibn Kathir has already told us that the noise-making of ayah 26 belongs to these disbelievers "and those who follow in their footsteps." Precedents keep collecting followers long after the one who set them has gone.

## Living it: the Muslim's opposite response

Immediately after explaining ayah 26, Ibn Kathir says: "Allah commanded us to be different from that," and cites the command in Sūrat al-Aʿrāf — **"So, when the Qur'an is recited, listen to it, and be silent that you may receive mercy"** (7:204).

Put the two verses side by side and the contrast is complete. They said: *do not listen, and make noise, that you may overcome.* Allah says: *listen, and be silent, that you may receive mercy.* Two postures towards the same recitation; two entirely different outcomes.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān draws the ruling out of this: "making noises with the intention of creating disturbance in the recitation of the Qur'an is a sign of disbelief," while "to listen quietly to the recitation of the Qur'an is *wajib* (necessary) and a sign of faith." (*Wajib* here means obligatory — not an optional courtesy.)

Then it turns the mirror on us, and the criticism is uncomfortably modern. Maʿārif observes that it has become a usual practice for people to put on the Qur'an loudly — "which can be heard in about every restaurant and place of gathering" — "while people go about their business never paying any attention to the Holy Qur'an." Its verdict: "This practice presents a picture that was a sign of infidels. May Allah Almighty guide Muslims."

The remedy it offers is practical, and it is two options, not one. In its own words, people "should either avoid the recitation of the Holy Qur'an at such places and on such occasions where people are unable to listen to it, or if they wish to benefit from the blessing of the recitation, they must listen to it quietly and attentively."

So: **either** do not play it where nobody can attend to it — **or**, if you want the blessing of it, actually listen.

The passage leaves a simple test. When the Qur'an is recited within your hearing — in the prayer, on a phone, in a car, in a gathering — does something in you go quiet? That silence is the exact opposite of ayah 26, and by the promise of 7:204 it is a doorway to mercy.

passages.title: Our Lord is Allah, then stand firm
passages.tafsir:
This passage is the Qur'an's short answer to the question "what does Allah actually want from a person?" — a sentence said with the tongue and meant with the whole life — and then it shows what that sentence earns: angels descending with comfort at the hardest moment, and a welcome-gift in Paradise from the One who forgives. Ayah 30 states the condition and the descent of the angels, ayah 31 records what the angels say, and ayah 32 names the Host who prepared the reception. The three hold together as one continuous statement: **one condition, one consequence.**

## Where we are in the surah

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān points out the turn. From the beginning of the surah the address has been to those who rejected the Qur'an, prophethood and the Oneness of Allah; with reference to the signs of Allah's omnipotence they were invited to believe in His Oneness, and then told of the evil fate of those who reject the life to come, with a detailed account of the punishment of Hell. **Now the text takes up the other side of the ledger** — the condition of the believing people and of those having perfect faith, their being honoured and exalted in this world and in eternity, along with some special directions for them. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān describes these believers as people who not only keep to the straight path and abide by the revealed laws themselves in their deeds and morals, but also call others towards Allah and care about their reformation.

## "Our Lord is Allah" — the claim behind the words

Ayah 30 names two qualities, not one. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān sets them out plainly: **affirming Allah as their Lord — that is faith (īmān); and the second, remaining steadfast — that is their good deeds.** The verse describes people who combine true faith with good practice.

What makes the first half true? Tafsir Kashshaf, quoted in Maʿārif ul Qurʼān, is searching here. A person's declaration that his Lord is Allah can only be true when he believes from the bottom of his heart that he is being brought up by Allah in all situations and at every step, that he cannot take even one breath without His mercy — and all this *demands* that one be so devoted and steadfast in his ways of worship that neither heart nor body deviates even a hair's breadth from submission to Him, like a slave. Said that way, the second half of the ayah is not an extra requirement bolted on to the first. **It is what the first half looks like when it is real.**

## Istiqāmah: the small word that holds the whole religion

The word the text uses for this second quality is *istiqāmah*, rendered in Maʿārif ul Qurʼān as "remaining steadfast," and discussed there under the heading "the sense of being upright." The classical authorities explain it from different angles, and Maʿārif ul Qurʼān lines them up:

- **Abū Bakr aṣ-Ṣiddīq** (may Allah be pleased with him): firmness in unshaken faith — the sense Maulana Thanawi takes, and an explanation Maʿārif ul Qurʼān reports from Abū Bakr. Ibn Kathir preserves the moment: Ibn Jarir recorded that Saʿīd bin ʿImrān said, "I read this ayah to Abū Bakr aṣ-Ṣiddīq," and he said, *"Those are the ones who do not associate anything with Allah."*
- **ʿUthmān** (may Allah be pleased with him): nearly the same — *ikhlāṣ*, sincerity in deeds.
- **ʿUmar** (may Allah be pleased with him), in words Maʿārif ul Qurʼān quotes from Tafsir Mazhari: *"Istiqāmah is that you hold on unwaveringly to all the injunctions of Allah — carry out the good deeds and stay away from prohibitions, and do not seek escape-routes like foxes."*
- **ʿAlī and Ibn ʿAbbās** (may Allah be pleased with them): the discharge of the obligatory duties.
- **Ḥasan al-Baṣrī**: to obey Allah in all deeds and to avoid His disobedience.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān, citing Tafsir Mazhari, judges ʿUmar's description the most comprehensive, and notes that Abū Bakr's and ʿUthmān's amount to the same thing, since sincerity in deeds is stressed by them along with good deeds. Al-Jaṣṣāṣ adopted this explanation, quoting Abul-ʿĀliyah, and so did Ibn Jarir.

Sit with ʿUmar's words for a moment. They cover two things at once: holding to the injunctions — doing the good, staying clear of the prohibited — and *not going looking for a way around them.* That second clause is why the definition reaches further than the others: it closes off not only the breaking of a command but the search for an exit from it.
