This is why, as Maʿārif ul Qurʼān says, the scholars called istiqāmah a small word that nonetheless comprises all the revealed laws of Islam: carrying out all the orders of Allah and staying away from all prohibitions and odious things — **on a permanent basis.**

Ibn Kathir reads the phrase the same way: they do good deeds sincerely for the sake of Allah, and they obey Allah, doing what He has prescribed for them. He also records a second exchange, from al-Aswad bin Hilāl: Abū Bakr aṣ-Ṣiddīq asked people what they said about this ayah, and they said, "They shun sin." He said, *"You have not interpreted it improperly."* Then he explained: they say "Our Lord is Allah," then they stand firm and do not turn to any other god besides Him. Ibn Kathir notes this was also the view of Mujāhid, ʿIkrimah, as-Suddī and others.

## What the Prophet ﷺ told Sufyān

Ibn Kathir records that Aḥmad reported from Sufyān bin ʿAbdullāh ath-Thaqafī: *"I said, 'O Messenger of Allah, tell me something that I can adhere to.'"* He ﷺ said:

> **قُلْ: رَبِّيَ اللهُ، ثُمَّ اسْتَقِمْ**
> *"Say, my Lord is Allah, then stand firm."*

Sufyān then asked what the Prophet ﷺ feared most for him. **The Messenger of Allah ﷺ took hold of the edge of his own tongue and said: "This."** Ibn Kathir notes it was also recorded by at-Tirmidhī and Ibn Mājah, and that at-Tirmidhī said, "Ḥasan Ṣaḥīḥ."

In the version Ibn Kathir attributes to Muslim in his Ṣaḥīḥ and to an-Nasāʾī, Sufyān asked for something about Islam that he would not have to ask anyone else about after him — and the answer was: *"Say: I believe in Allah, then stand firm."* Maʿārif ul Qurʼān relates the same hadith, citing Muslim, and renders it: *"Say, 'I have faith in Allah', and then remain steadfast to it."*

Two things are worth noticing. First, **the Prophet ﷺ answered a request for the whole of Islam by quoting the shape of this ayah**: a declaration, then steadfastness on it. Second, when a man who had just been told to stand firm asked what most endangered him, he was not pointed to anything distant or exotic. He was pointed to something inside his own mouth.

## "The angels descend upon them"

The reward begins in ayah 30 with *tatanazzalu ʿalayhim al-malāʾikah* — the angels come down upon them. **When?** The commentators differ, and the difference is worth knowing because each view opens a different comfort.

- **At the moment of death.** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān reports this from Ibn ʿAbbās, and Ibn Kathir cites Mujāhid, as-Suddī, Zayd bin Aslam and Zayd's son for the same.
- **On the Day of Resurrection**, at the time of rising from the graves — reported from Qatādah, and Ibn Kathir mentions this view too.
- **On three occasions** — at death, in the graves, and at the rising from the graves. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān reports this from Wakīʿ ibn al-Jarrāḥ; Ibn Kathir reports it from Zayd bin Aslam, recorded by Ibn Abi Hatim, and says: *"this view reconciles all the opinions; it is a good view and it is true."*
- **Continuously, even now.** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān relays Abū Ḥayyān's view in *al-Baḥr al-Muḥīṭ*: angels in fact keep descending upon the believers all the time, even in this life, and their effects and blessings are found in the deeds of the believers — but they will be visible on those occasions only, and it is then that the voice of the angels will be heard.

That last opinion changes how the ayah feels. On Abū Ḥayyān's reading, the steadfast believer is *already* accompanied; what death and resurrection change is not the company but the ability to perceive it.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān also relays, from Abū Nuʿaym, that Thābit al-Bunānī, when he reached this ayah while reciting Sūrah Ḥā Mīm Sajdah, said that according to a report that had reached them, the believer at the time of rising from his grave on the Day of Resurrection will be met by **the two angels who used to be with him in the world**, and they will console him not to worry or be afraid but to be happy with the glad tidings of Paradise that was promised to him — and these words of the angels will bring serenity to the believer.

## What the angels say

Their speech has a precise architecture, and Ibn Kathir unpacks it:

**"Fear not"** — Mujāhid, ʿIkrimah and Zayd bin Aslam explain this as: do not fear that which you will face in the Hereafter. Fear faces forward.

**"Nor grieve"** — do not grieve for what you have left behind of worldly things: children, family, wealth, and debt — *"for we will take care of it for you."* Grief faces backward. Between the two phrases, **the anxieties of a dying person are met from both directions**, and notice how ordinary and domestic the list is: the people who depend on you, the money you owed. The angels do not tell the believer these things do not matter. They tell him they are handled.

**"Receive the glad tidings of Paradise which you have been promised"** — so, as Ibn Kathir puts it, they give glad tidings of the end of bad things and the arrival of good things. He compares this to what is said in the hadith narrated by al-Barāʾ (may Allah be pleased with him), that the angels say to the soul of the believer: *"Come out, O good soul, from the good body in which you used to dwell; come out to rest, and provision, and a Lord Who is not angry."*

Note the word "promised." Nothing new is being offered at death. **The angels are confirming delivery on what was said long before.**

## "We are your allies" — ayah 31

*Awliyāʾ* is the word — rendered "friends" and "supporters," and glossed by Ibn Kathir as *close companions*. Ibn Kathir explains that the angels will say to the believers when death approaches: we have been your friends, your close companions, in this world, protecting you and helping you **by the command of Allah** — and we will be with you in the Hereafter, keeping you from feeling lonely in your graves and when the Trumpet is blown; we will reassure you on the Day of Resurrection, take you across the Ṣirāṭ, and bring you to the Gardens of delight.

Read that as an itinerary. **Grave, Trumpet, Judgment, the Ṣirāṭ, the Garden** — the entire terrifying route is named, and at every stage a companion is named with it. The believer is told, in advance, that he will not travel any of it alone.

## Everything you desire, and things you never thought to want

Ayah 31 gives two clauses. Ibn Kathir: *"Therein you shall have all that your souls desire"* means in Paradise you will have all that you wish for and that will delight you; and *"therein you shall have all for which you ask"* means whatever you ask for will appear before you as you wish it to be.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān draws the two together neatly: **all your desires will be fulfilled, whether you request them or not.**

Then ayah 32 names the manner of the giving: *nuzulan* — rendered "an entertainment" or "hospitality," but, as Mufti Muhammad Taqi Usmani notes in Maʿārif ul Qurʼān, better translated as a **welcome-gift**, since the word originally means *a thing prepared by a host to be offered to him soon after his arrival.* Maʿārif ul Qurʼān draws out the implication: many of the delights provided there will be such that desire for them had not even entered your heart — as happens to a guest, especially the guest of a great personage, that many things are presented to him which he had not even imagined.

That is the force of the word. **A welcome-gift is not the whole of the hospitality; it is what is waiting the moment you walk in.** If this is the reception, what is the residence?

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān cites two hadith to make the immediacy concrete. It states that the Prophet ﷺ said that in Paradise, if the desire comes into your heart to eat the flesh of a flying bird you are looking at, it would immediately fall in front of you completely cooked and ready to eat — some narrations having it that the bird would not have been touched by fire or smoke, yet would come down already cooked (Maʿārif ul Qurʼān cites al-Bazzār and al-Bayhaqī, narrated by Ibn Masʿūd, via Mazharī). And in another, that if a believer in Paradise wishes to have a child born in his house, the conception, delivery, weaning and growing into being an adult would all take place in a moment (cited from Tirmidhī, Bayhaqī and others, via Mazharī). The point in both is not the bird or the child. **It is that in Paradise the gap between wanting and having closes to nothing.**

## The two Names at the end

The passage closes by naming the Host: **al-Ghafūr, ar-Raḥīm** — the Oft-Forgiving, the Most Merciful. Ibn Kathir explains the whole reception as *"a welcoming gift and a blessing from the One Who has forgiven your sins and Who is Merciful and Kind towards you, Who has forgiven you, concealed your faults and been Kind and Merciful."*

This is the passage's final act of realism. Ayah 30 asked for istiqāmah — commands kept and prohibitions avoided, and on a permanent basis. No honest reader finishes that description feeling he has achieved it. **So the passage does not sign off with a name of justice or exact reckoning. It signs off with forgiveness and mercy** — and with the detail that Allah has *concealed* the faults He forgave. The steadfast do not enter Paradise because their record was spotless. They enter because the One who kept their record chose to cover it.

## Living it

The passage is unusually direct about what it asks:

1. **Say it, and mean it as a claim on your whole life.** Per Kashshaf, "Our Lord is Allah" is only true when you believe from the bottom of your heart that you cannot take even one breath without His mercy.
2. **Guard the tongue.** Asked what he feared most for a man told to stand firm, the Prophet ﷺ took hold of the edge of his tongue and said, "This."
3. **Stop looking for escape-routes.** ʿUmar's definition is the practical test: hold to the commands and the prohibitions, and do not go hunting for a way around them.
4. **Take istiqāmah as permanent, not seasonal** — the scholars, per Maʿārif ul Qurʼān, described it as all the orders of Allah carried out and all prohibitions avoided *on a permanent basis.*
5. **Let it settle your fear of dying.** Whatever you would fear ahead and grieve behind — the family, the wealth, the debt — the angels' two sentences are aimed at exactly those two anxieties.
6. **Do not measure the reward by what you can currently imagine.** The word is *nuzul*: a welcome-gift, including things desire for which had never entered your heart.

passages.title: Repel evil with what is better
passages.tafsir:
These four ayat describe the one who calls people to Allah — and then hand him one of the hardest instructions in the Qur'an: when people answer your call with insult, answer their insult with kindness. Ayah 33 paints the portrait; ayat 34–36 are the training that makes the portrait possible.

What holds the passage together is a single arc: **who you are (33) → how you respond (34) → why almost no one manages it (35) → what to do when the pressure comes from inside you (36).** As Maʿārif ul Qurʼān puts it, the special instructions for those engaged in calling others towards Allah begin at ayah 34. Ayah 33 is not a standalone compliment; it is the job description, and the rest is the code of conduct.

## Ayah 33 — the best speech on earth

*"And who is better in speech than he who invites to Allah, and does righteous deeds, and says: 'I am one of the Muslims.'"*

The question is rhetorical, and Ibn Kathir takes the phrase **"invites to Allah"** at its plainest: *he calls the servants of Allah to Him.* Not to himself, not to a party or a personality — to Allah. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān draws the conclusion the wording invites: the best and most excellent discourse a man can produce is to call others towards truth. It also notes what stage of the believer's life this describes — this is the second aspect of the state of the totally obedient believers: they do not only have faith and do good deeds themselves, they invite others to do the same. And it explicitly includes **every medium** — the spoken word, writing, or any other manner of calling. Nothing in the ayah restricts the honour to a pulpit.

Notice, though, that Allah does not stop at speech. Three things are named, in order:

**1. He invites to Allah.** The outward work.

**2. "And does righteous deeds."** Ibn Kathir explains: *he himself follows that which he says, so it benefits him as well as others.* He is not one of those who enjoin good but do not do it themselves, or forbid evil yet do it themselves. He does good and avoids evil, and calls people to their Creator. This is the hinge of the ayah. The praise is not for the message alone but for a life that matches it.

**3. "And says: 'I am one of the Muslims.'"** He owns the identity publicly — placing himself *among* those who submit to Allah.

Ibn Kathir concludes that the ayah is **general in meaning** and applies to everyone who calls people to what is good and is himself guided by what he says — and that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ is the foremost among people in this regard, as Muhammad bin Sirin, As-Suddi and ʿAbdur-Rahman bin Zayd bin Aslam said.

**Al-Hasan Al-Basri's reading.** ʿAbdur-Razzaq narrated from Maʿmar that Al-Hasan Al-Basri recited this ayah and said: *"This is the beloved of Allah, this is the close friend of Allah, this is the chosen one of Allah, this is the most beloved of all the people of earth to Allah. He responded to the call of Allah and called mankind to that to which he had responded. He did righteous deeds in response and said, 'I am one of the Muslims.' This is Allah's Khalifah."* The sequence in his words is worth pausing on: **he responded first**, then called mankind to what he had already answered. He is not directing traffic down a road he has never walked.

## A genuine difference of opinion: is this ayah about the mu'adhdhin?

Here the two commentaries in front of us take different paths, and it is worth seeing both rather than flattening them.

**The view that it refers to the one who calls the adhan.** Ibn Kathir reports this as a stated opinion — that what is meant is the righteous mu'adhdhin — citing what is mentioned in **Sahih Muslim**: *"The Mu'adhdhins will be the ones with the longest necks on the Day of Resurrection."* He also cites what is reported **in As-Sunan**, that the Prophet ﷺ said: *"The Imam is a guarantor and the Mu'adhdhin is in a position of trust. May Allah guide the Imams and forgive the Mu'adhdhin."*

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān leans into this reading: the one who calls the adhan is included in this category, because he calls others towards prayer. It relates that **Sayyidah ʿA'ishah** (may Allah be pleased with her) said this verse is about the mu'adhdhins, and that *"and acts righteously"* here means the offering of two rakʿahs of prayer between the adhan and the iqamah. It adds a narration that the Prophet ﷺ said that **the supplication between adhan and iqamah is not rejected** (Abu Dawud and Tirmidhi, narrated by Sayyidna Anas, may Allah be pleased with him — via Mazhari). And it notes an important condition on the great merits and blessings of the adhan and its reply: that the adhan be **proclaimed purely for Allah, and not for any payment or compensation.**

**Ibn Kathir's argument for generality.** He holds the correct view to be that the ayah is general and *includes* the mu'adhdhin along with everyone else — and he gives a historical reason. **When this ayah was revealed, the adhan had not been prescribed at all.** The ayah was revealed in Makkah; the adhan was prescribed in Al-Madinah after the Hijrah, when it was shown to ʿAbdullah bin ʿAbd Rabbihi Al-Ansari in a dream. He told the Messenger of Allah ﷺ about it, and he told him to teach it to Bilal (may Allah be pleased with him), who had a more beautiful voice.

The two positions are not as far apart as they look: the one who calls the adhan is on any reading someone who calls others towards prayer, and Ibn Kathir's generality includes him. What Ibn Kathir resists is narrowing the honour to one office.

## Ayah 34 — "Good and evil are not equal"

*"The good deed and the evil deed cannot be equal. Repel (the evil) with one which is better, then verily he, between whom and you there was enmity, (will become) as though he was a close friend."*

Ibn Kathir's gloss on the opening clause is short and absolute: **there is a huge difference between them.** The Qur'an will not let you treat a wrong done to you and your response to it as two moves in the same game. They are not on the same moral plane, and so they should not be traded one for one.

**"Repel with that which is better."** Ibn Kathir: *when someone does you wrong, repel him by treating him well.* Maʿārif ul Qurʼān presses the point further, and it is the most practical sentence in the whole passage: it is certainly good not to repay evil with evil and to forgive — **but it is much better to do some good to the wrongdoer after forgiving him.** Forgiveness cancels the debt; actively doing him good opens a door. The ayah is asking for the second. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān sums up the whole set of instructions this way: not to repay evil with evil, but to be patient and to be obliging — so that the settled habit of one who calls others to Allah is to reply to their bad behaviour in the best possible manner.

**ʿUmar's line.** Ibn Kathir cites ʿUmar (may Allah be pleased with him): *"There is no better punishment for one who has disobeyed Allah with regard to you, than your obeying Allah with regard to him."* This is a complete reframe of revenge. Your response is not primarily about the other person at all — it is an act of obedience to Allah, performed in his direction. That single shift is what makes the command survivable.

**The promised outcome.** Ibn Kathir on *"as though he was a close friend"*: *if you treat well those who treat you badly, this good deed will lead to reconciliation, love and empathy, and it will be as if he is a close friend to you, and he will feel pity for you and be kind to you.* Reconciliation, love, empathy, pity, kindness — that is the whole distance the ayah promises to travel, starting from enmity.

**Sayyidna Ibn ʿAbbas's summary** (may Allah be pleased with him). Reported by ʿAli bin Abi Talhah and cited by Ibn Kathir, and echoed in Maʿārif ul Qurʼān from Mazhari, it breaks the command into three concrete situations — Allah commands the believers:

- **to be patient when they feel angry** — to be patient with the one who is expressing his anger with you;
- **to be forbearing when confronted with ignorance** — to be tolerant with the one who is being ignorant with you;
- **and to forgive when they are mistreated** — to forgive the one who has made you suffer.

And the promise attached: *if they do this, Allah will save them from the Shaytan and subdue their enemies to them until they become like close friends.*

**A worked example.** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān relates from Qurtubi that some narrations mention a man who abused or reviled Sayyidna Abu Bakr (may Allah be pleased with him), and Abu Bakr answered him: *"If what you are saying is true — that I am at fault and am bad — then I pray Allah Taʿala to forgive me; and if you have told a lie, then may Allah forgive you."* Both halves of the reply are prayers. There is no counter-insult in it anywhere, and no self-defence either: the criticism is taken seriously as possible truth about himself, and the critic is left with a supplication.

## Ayah 35 — why almost no one does this

*"But none is granted it except those who are patient; and none is granted it except the owner of the great portion."*

The ayah is realistic about its own difficulty. Ibn Kathir: *no one accepts this advice and works according to it, except for those who can be patient in doing so — for it is difficult for people to do.* That last clause is a mercy. If you find this hard, the Qur'an has already said so.

Two conditions are named, and they are worth distinguishing:

**"Those who are patient."** Patience is the entry requirement — and Ibn Kathir's words make clear what kind of patience is meant: not a mood, but the capacity to keep accepting this advice and acting on it in the very situations where it is hardest.

**"The owner of the great portion."** Ibn Kathir explains this as *the one who has a great portion of happiness in this world and in the Hereafter.* This reframes the whole passage: what looks like loss — swallowing an insult, spending kindness on someone who has earned none — is described by Allah as receiving a *great portion*. The world's arithmetic says you lost the exchange. Allah's says you were handed a fortune.

And note how both clauses are worded: none is **granted** it. It is spoken of as something received, twice over. So the natural response is to ask Allah for it.

## Ayah 36 — the enemy you cannot be kind to

*"And if an evil whisper from Shaytan tries to turn you away, then seek refuge in Allah. Verily, He is the All-Hearer, the All-Knower."*

This is the ayah that makes the passage workable, and Ibn Kathir's explanation of *why it comes here* is the sharpest insight in the whole section:

> *the devils among men may be deceived by your kind treatment of him, but the devils among the Jinn, when they insinuate their evil whispers, cannot be dealt with except by seeking refuge with the Creator Who gave him power over you.*

So there are two kinds of adversary and two entirely different strategies. **The human antagonist** can be won over — kindness disarms him, and ayah 34 has just told you how. **The satanic whisper** cannot be won over. You cannot be gracious to a whisper; it has no heart to soften. Against it there is exactly one move, and it is not a technique of self-control but an act of worship: *seek refuge in Allah.* Ibn Kathir adds the promise: *if you seek refuge with Allah and turn to Him, He will stop him from harming you and bring his efforts to naught.*

The believer, then, is not told to be surprised when the urge to strike back surges up in him. He is told in advance what to do in the second it arrives.

**The two Names at the close.** The ayah ends by naming Allah the All-Hearer, the All-Knower. He **hears** the words of refuge you say, and He **knows** what is happening inside you that no witness saw. The refuge is heard and the whisper is known, both by Him.

**From the Sunnah.** Ibn Kathir records that when the Messenger of Allah ﷺ stood up to pray, he would say: *"I seek refuge in Allah the All-Hearing, All-Knowing, from the accursed Shaytan and his evil insinuations, breath and impurity."* The wording of his ﷺ refuge mirrors the wording of the ayah — *the All-Hearing, All-Knowing* — which is a small lesson in itself: seek refuge in Allah by the very Names He gave you here.

**The Qur'an's own cross-references.** Ibn Kathir notes that there is nothing like this in the Qur'an apart from two other passages — Surat Al-Aʿraf: *"Show forgiveness, enjoin what is good, and turn away from the foolish. And if an evil whisper comes to you from Shaytan, then seek refuge with Allah. Verily, He is All-Hearer, All-Knower"* (7:199–200); and Surat Al-Mu'minun: *"Repel evil with that which is better. We are Best-Acquainted with the things they utter. And say: 'My Lord! I seek refuge with You from the whisperings of the Shayatin. And I seek refuge with You, my Lord, lest they should come near me'"* (23:96–98). In all three places the shape is the same: **the instruction on how to bear with people is immediately followed by the command to seek refuge.** The Qur'an never issues this instruction without also handing you the defence.

## Living it

Read as one unit, the passage gives a believer who wants to call others to Allah a short, demanding rule of life:

1. **Say it, and be it.** Your credibility is your conduct (ayah 33). Whatever the medium — speech, writing, or any other manner (Maʿārif ul Qurʼān) — the message only works if you have already responded to it yourself, as Al-Hasan Al-Basri said.
2. **Do not price your response off theirs.** Good and evil are not equal — there is a huge difference between them — so do not trade them at par (ayah 34).
3. **Go one step past forgiving.** It is good not to repay evil with evil and to forgive; it is much better to do some good to the wrongdoer after forgiving him (Maʿārif ul Qurʼān).
4. **Reframe the target of the act.** ʿUmar's rule: your kindness is obedience to Allah in his direction, not a favour he deserved.
5. **Expect it to be hard, and expect it to pay.** Ibn Kathir says plainly that it is difficult for people to do (ayah 35) — and the ayah calls whoever is granted it the owner of a great portion, a great portion of happiness in this world and in the Hereafter.
6. **When the urge to hit back flares, do not argue with it — seek refuge.** What you are facing there is not the human being in front of you (ayah 36). And ask Allah for this quality itself, since the ayah speaks of it as something granted.

passages.title: Sun, moon and the reviving earth
passages.tafsir:
## What this passage is about

These three ayat take the reader outside — to the turning of night into day, to the sun and the moon overhead, and to a dead field that turns green after rain — and then ask one question of it all: if these are *signs*, why bow to the sign instead of the One who made it? Ayah 37 shows the signs and forbids prostrating to them; ayah 38 answers the proud who refuse; ayah 39 takes the same evidence and pushes it one step further, to the raising of the dead. What holds the three together is a single movement: **from the created thing, to the Creator, to the Day He will bring you back.**

Ibn Kathir sums up the purpose of the whole passage in one line: here Allah reminds His creation of His power, that He is the One who has no equal, and that He is able to do all things.

## Ayah 37: four signs you have never once been without

"And from among His signs are the night and the day, and the sun and the moon."

Ibn Kathir unpacks each piece. Allah created **the night with its darkness and the day with its light**, and — in Ibn Kathir's words — they alternate without ceasing. He created **the sun with its shining light** and **the moon with its reflected light** — two very different kinds of luminance, one blazing of itself, one borrowing.

Then a detail worth pausing on: Allah "allotted their stages and gave them separate orbits in the heavens." Ibn Kathir explains *why* — so that by the variations in their movements a human being can know:

- the stages of night and day,
- weeks, months and years,
- and the time periods related to **people's rights, acts of worship and various transactions**.

That last clause repays a moment's thought. The sun and moon are not decoration; Ibn Kathir names them as the means by which those three kinds of period are known. A right one person holds over another falls due by them. An act of worship enters and leaves its time by them. A transaction is dated and matures by them.

**Why single out the sun and moon?** Ibn Kathir gives the reason: because they are the most beautiful of the heavenly bodies that can be seen in both the upper and lower realms. So Allah points out that they are *created entities*, "in a state of enthrallment to Him, subject to His dominion and control." The two most striking things in the sky are, on Ibn Kathir's reading, precisely the two things shown to be made, held and ruled.

## The turn: "Do not prostrate to the sun, nor to the moon"

"…but prostrate yourselves to Allah who created them, if you (really) worship Him."

Notice the logic. The passage does not first argue at length that Allah exists and then forbid sun-worship. It presents the sun and moon as created and subject to His control, and the prohibition follows from it: you cannot worship what is itself under His dominion while claiming to serve Him.

Ibn Kathir's gloss on the closing condition is sharp: *do not associate anything in worship with Him, for your worship of Him will be of no benefit to you if you worship others alongside Him, because He does not forgive the association of others in worship with Him.* This is the crux. Worship offered to Allah *and* to something else is not partial credit; on this reading it brings no benefit at all. Tawhid — devoting worship to Allah alone — is not a majority stake. It is the whole of it.

## The ruling that follows: sajdah belongs to Allah alone

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān draws the legal conclusion directly from ayah 37: **prostration is the right of the Creator of the universe alone.** The consensus of the Ummah is that prostrating before any star, human being, and so on is harām (forbidden), whether it is done as worship or merely as a gesture of respect and reverence.

Maʿārif then makes a careful distinction that a reader should not blur:

- Whoever prostrates before other than Allah **intending to worship him** thereby becomes an unbeliever.
- Whoever prostrates **simply as a mark of respect and reverence** is not called an unbeliever — but he is guilty of committing a serious harām act and is a sinner.

And it addresses the obvious objection. Was prostration to a creature not permitted before? Maʿārif answers on two levels. **Prostration of worship** to any being other than Allah has never been lawful for any nation, in the sharīʿah of any prophet, because it amounts to shirk (associating partners with Allah), and shirk has never been allowed in any revealed code. **Prostration in respect and reverence**, with no intention of worship, had been allowed in the codes revealed to some prophets: all the angels were ordered to prostrate before Sayyidnā Ādam (peace be upon him) before he came into this world, and the Qur'an states that the father and brothers of Sayyidnā Yūsuf (peace be upon him) prostrated before him. But the jurists of this Ummah are unanimous that such prostration was permissible in the earlier codes only, and **it stands abrogated in Islam**. Prostration for any being other than Allah has been declared absolutely harām. (Maʿārif notes that the author gave full details in his booklet in Arabic, المقالۃ المرضیۃ فی حکم سجدۃ التحیۃ — *Al-maqalat-ul-mardiyyah, fi Hukmi sajdat-it-tahiyyah* — of which an Urdu translation has also been published.)

## Ayah 38: "But if they are too proud…"

"But if they are too proud, then there are those who are with your Lord who glorify Him night and day, and never are they tired."

Ibn Kathir explains what exactly they are too proud for: **to worship Him alone** — insisting instead on associating others with Him. Pride here is not an incidental fault alongside their disbelief; it is what stands between them and worshipping Allah by Himself.

"Those who are with your Lord" — Ibn Kathir identifies them: **the angels.** They glorify Him by night and by day, and never are they tired.

The point is one of the most humbling in the surah. If a person will not bow, the worship of Allah does not pause for his absence. Ibn Kathir places alongside it the ayah, *"But if these disbelieve therein, then indeed We have entrusted it to a people who are not disbelievers therein"* (6:89). Allah is not short of worshippers. A creation that glorifies Him night and day, without tiring, is already in place. The proud man who withholds his forehead from the dust harms only himself; the praise continues over his head, and he is simply not part of it.

There is also a quiet rebuke folded into the pairing. The angels glorify Him "night and day" — the very night and day named in ayah 37 as signs. The signs themselves keep the schedule of worship. Only the human being holds out.

## The sajdah of recitation — and where exactly to make it

Ayah 38 carries the sajdah mark. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān explains that this is one of the "verses of sajdah," the recitation of which makes prostration obligatory upon the one who recites them and the one who listens to them. This is called the **sajdah of tilāwah** (the prostration of recitation).

There is consensus in the Ummah that a sajdah of tilāwah is wājib (obligatory) in this surah. **The scholars differ only over the exact place where it becomes wājib**, and Maʿārif reports the difference carefully rather than settling it:

- **At the end of ayah 37** — after *in kuntum iyyāhu taʿbudūn* ("if it is Him whom you worship"). Qāḍī Abū Bakr Ibn al-ʿArabī has written in *Aḥkām al-Qurʼān* that Sayyidnā ʿAlī and Sayyidnā Ibn Masʿūd (may Allah be pleased with them) used to prostrate here, and **Imām Mālik** adopted this very stance.
- **At the end of ayah 38** — after *lā yas'amūn* ("and they do not get weary"). Sayyidnā Ibn ʿAbbās (may Allah be pleased with him) used to prostrate here; Sayyidnā ʿAbdullāh ibn ʿUmar (may Allah be pleased with him) also advised prostration at this place. Masrūq, Abū ʿAbd al-Raḥmān al-Sulamī, Ibrāhīm al-Nakhaʿī, Ibn Sīrīn, Qatādah and others — and most jurists — used to prostrate at ayah 38. Imām Abū Bakr al-Jaṣṣāṣ has said in *Aḥkām al-Qurʼān* that this has been the view of all the leading Hanafi scholars.

**The practical way through the disagreement**, as al-Jaṣṣāṣ reasons it: in view of the differences, it is on the safer side to prostrate at the end of ayah 38. If prostration becomes wājib at the end of ayah 37, the obligation is still discharged by performing it after the recitation of ayah 38; and if it becomes wājib at ayah 38, then its discharge there is more obvious still.

There is a beautiful fit between the ruling and the passage. The ayah forbids prostrating to the sun and moon and commands prostrating to Allah — and the believer who reaches it in recitation does not merely read the command, he **obeys it on the spot**, putting his face on the ground while the words about the tireless angels are still in the air.

## Ayah 39: the dead field and the dead man

"And among His signs is that you see the earth barren, but when We send down water to it, it is stirred to life and growth. Verily, He who gives it life is surely able to give life to the dead. Indeed, He is able to do all things."

Ibn Kathir tells us what this new sign is a sign *of*: "signs of **His ability to bring the dead back to life**." Ayah 37 offered signs of Allah's power and His having no equal; here the evidence is aimed squarely at resurrection.

On *khāshiʿah*, rendered "barren," Ibn Kathir is spare and vivid: it means **lifeless, with nothing growing in it; it is dead.** Not merely dry — dead. And *ihtazzat wa rabat*, "it is stirred to life and growth," means, says Ibn Kathir, that **it brings forth all kinds of crops and fruits**.

Then comes the argument, stated by Allah Himself so that no one has to construct it: *"Verily, He who gives it life is surely able to give life to the dead."* And the ayah stresses that you have watched this happen — *annaka tarā*, "**that you see** the earth barren." The resurrection is not asking you to believe in something unprecedented. It is asking you to admit that what you already watch every season is exactly what you call impossible when it involves you.

The passage then closes at the widest possible altitude: *"Indeed, He is able to do all things."* The rain-and-earth example makes the point, but Allah does not leave His power resting on the example. Reviving the earth is one demonstration of an ability that has no limit at all.

## Living it

**Read the sky as a signature, not a subject.** Ibn Kathir's method is to take the most beautiful bodies visible in the heavens and point out that they are created, held in enthrallment to Allah, subject to His dominion and control. The splendour is real; the ayah simply refuses to let it be the last word.

**Keep your worship undivided.** Ibn Kathir's warning stands over the whole passage: worship of Allah brings no benefit to a person who worships others alongside Him. Examine what you actually turn to in fear and hope.

**Guard the sajdah.** By the consensus Maʿārif reports, the forehead on the ground belongs to Allah alone — not to a star, not to any created being, not even as a courtesy. What was permitted as a mark of respect in earlier codes is abrogated in this one.

**Do not be the one who is too proud.** Ayah 38 is a mirror. The angels glorify Allah night and day and are never tired. Whether you join that praise or stand outside it changes nothing for Allah; it decides only where you stand.

**Let the rain preach.** Ibn Kathir reads ayah 39 as a sign of Allah's ability to bring the dead back to life. So the next time you see a field green up after a dry season, take the ayah's own step: the One who did that is "able to give life to the dead," and "He is able to do all things."

passages.title: Falsehood cannot approach this Book
passages.tafsir:
These three ayat move from the people who twist Allah's revelation to the Book they are trying to twist. Ayah 40 exposes a particular kind of rejection — one that hides itself — and warns that it is fully visible to Allah; ayat 41–42 answer it by describing the Qur'an itself as a Book so honoured and so guarded that falsehood cannot reach it from any direction.

## Ayah 40: a crookedness that thinks it is invisible

The passage opens with a word worth slowing down for: **yulḥidūna**, from the root of *ilḥād*. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān explains its lexical sense as **to deviate, to incline towards one side, to be crooked**. Applied to Allah's āyāt, it is not a straight, honest "no". It is a swerve.

Two of the earliest explanations sit side by side in Ibn Kathir:

- **Ibn ʿAbbas**: "Al-Ilḥād means putting words in their improper places" — taking a statement and setting it down where it does not belong.
- **Qatadah and others**: "It means disbelief and obstinate behaviour" — open rejection and stubborn resistance.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān notes that the word lexically covers both — outright denial and denial dressed as interpretation — but that in the usage of the Qur'an and Sunnah, *ilḥād* is generally used for the second: a deviation that **apparently professes faith in the Qur'an and its verses**, yet assigns the Qur'an self-assumed meanings that go against the clear and explicit meanings accepted and recognised by the majority of the ummah, until the intent of the Qur'an is changed altogether. Maʿārif sums it up as "a kind of hypocritical kufr" — one that claims faith in the Book while fabricating meanings for it against the explicit provisions of the Qur'an, Sunnah and the principles of Islam.

That is why the clause that follows lands the way it does. **"They are not hidden from Us"** (*lā yakhfawna ʿalaynā*). Maʿārif ul Qurʼān draws attention to the wording: these words indicate that *ilḥād* was a kind of kufr that they **wanted to hide** — so Allah answers that they could not hide it from Him. The open denier at least declares himself. The one committing *ilḥād* has built a shelter of pious-sounding interpretation to stand in. The ayah removes the shelter. Ibn Kathir calls this "a stern warning and dire threat," stating that Allah — exalted is He — knows who denies **His signs, His Names and His attributes**, and that He will punish them for that.

**The two figures.** The rhetorical question that follows — *"Is he who is cast into the Fire better, or he who comes secure on the Day of Resurrection?"* — sets two people side by side and lets the contrast do the work. Ibn Kathir answers it in a single line: are these two equal? **They are not equal.**

**"Do what you will."** Mujahid, Ad-Dahhak and ʿAta' Al-Khurasani all read *iʿmalū mā shi'tum* as **a threat**, not a permission: do what you will of good or evil, for He knows and sees all that you do. The ayah seals it with **"Verily, He is All-Seer of what you do"** — *Baṣīr*, the All-Seeing.

## Ayah 41: the sentence that hangs on the same verdict

Ayah 41 begins a new "Indeed, those who…" — *"Indeed, those who disbelieved in the Reminder when it came to them."* Ad-Dahhak, As-Suddi and Qatadah are agreed on what "the Reminder" (*adh-dhikr*) means here: **this is the Qur'an**.

But read on and the sentence seems to break off — where is its predicate? Maʿārif ul Qurʼān reports that most exegetes resolve it grammatically: this clause is a **complement of the earlier phrase** in ayah 40, "those who go crooked about Our signs," and therefore, according to Arabic grammar, falls under the **same predicate** — *are not hidden from Us*. So the meaning runs: these people **cannot be hidden from Us, and consequently cannot escape the scourge.**

That grammatical link is the hinge of the whole passage. The twisters and the deniers are one file of people, and the verdict on them is one verdict.

**"And verily, it is an honourable, well-fortified, respected Book."** The word is **ʿazīz** — Ibn Kathir glosses it as meaning the Book is **protected and preserved, and nobody can produce anything like it**. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān, narrating from Ibn ʿAbbas through Tafsir Mazhari, gives the same sense: Allah **holds this Book dear and fully protected**; no falsehood can enter it. *ʿAzīz* thus carries both halves at once — precious and unassailable, the way something is guarded precisely because it is treasured.

## Ayah 42: no way in, front or back

*"Falsehood cannot come to it from before it or behind it."* Ibn Kathir's gloss is short and total: **there is no way to corrupt it**, because it has been sent down by the Lord of the worlds.

The commentators then open up the two words that make the ayah so complete.

**Who is "falsehood"?** Qatadah and As-Suddi say *bāṭil* here means **Shayṭan**, and "neither from its front nor from behind it" means **from any side**: Satan's manipulation and contrivance simply do not work on this Book — he cannot distort it by adding something to it or deleting something from it. The author of Tafsir Mazhari, after quoting this explanation, adds that the satans meant here include **both the satans of the jinn and of men** — neither can carry out any change or distortion in the Qur'an.

**Abu Ḥayyan**, in *Al-Baḥr ul-Muḥīṭ*, widens it further: the word *bāṭil* is not specific to Shayṭan. **Any falsehood or falsifier, whether from Shayṭan or from any other source, cannot succeed in the Qur'an.**

**From which two directions?** Abu Ḥayyan, referring to **Ṭabari**, gives the reading Maʿārif ul Qurʼān considers very appropriate here: a disbeliever can **neither dare to carry out any change in this Book openly, nor distort its meaning through *ilḥād* covertly**. And that is exactly the two doors:

- **"From before it"** — the frontal attack: a disbeliever tries openly to add something to the Qur'an or delete something from it.
- **"From behind it"** — the attack from the rear: somebody claiming to have faith tries covertly to distort the meaning of the Qur'an through false interpretations.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān makes the reason this reading is so apt explicit: there can be only two ways of introducing distortion or *ilḥād* into the Qur'an — through the wording, or through the meaning — and the ayah closes both. Whenever any wretched person attempted it, he had to face ignominy, and the Qur'an remained pure and untouched by his plans.

**How the protection is visible.** For the words, says Maʿārif ul Qurʼān, everybody can see it: the Qur'an has been read and recited throughout the world for fourteen centuries and **fully memorised by hundreds of thousands of people**; if anybody makes even the slightest mistake, the young, the old, the learned scholars, the unlettered — thousands upon thousands of Muslims raise their voice for correction. Maʿārif's note here names one attempt specifically: **Rawāfiḍ**, a term it says is used for the extremists among the Shi'ites — some of whom tried to add ten parts (*ajzāʼ*) and some particular verses — **but none could succeed.**

For the meanings, the point is more striking. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān argues that "from behind it" shows that the protection Allah Himself undertook, **"And indeed, We are there to protect it"** (15:9), is **not limited to its words only**. The pronoun "it" there points to the Qur'an, and the Qur'an is not just the name of words, but the name of words **and** meanings together. So Allah safeguarded its meanings and injunctions too — through His Messenger ﷺ and through his direct disciples, the noble Companions — such that if anyone attempts to distort it through false explanations, thousands of scholars stand up to refute him and he faces rejection. The commentary adds that it is clearly mentioned in correct ahadith that **a group will always remain among the Muslims, till the Last Day, who expose the distortions of those who commit *ilḥād* and clarify the correct meaning of the Qur'an.** Such people may hide their kufr from the whole world, but they cannot hide it from Allah — and since He is aware of their scheming, they are bound to face punishment.

**"Sent down by the All-Wise, Worthy of all praise."** The ayah's closing names two attributes as the reason for everything just said. Ibn Kathir: He is **Ḥakīm** — Wise in all that He says and does; and **Ḥamīd** — Praiseworthy in all that He commands and forbids, so that everything He does is for praiseworthy purposes and its consequences will be good. A Book from such a source is not a text anyone can improve, correct, or embarrass.

## The scholars on how far *ilḥād* goes

Because ayah 40 makes false interpretation a form of kufr, Maʿārif ul Qurʼān pauses on a real question of theology, and it is worth reporting carefully rather than flattening.

There is a known rule in the books of Islamic theology that a **mutaʼawwil** — someone who adheres to a wrong belief on the pretext of a different interpretation of the Qur'an and Sunnah — should not be declared a disbeliever. Maʿārif argues this rule cannot be taken so generally, since the idolaters too had a pretext, quoted in the Qur'an itself: *"And we do not worship them except that they may bring us closer to Allah"* (39:3) — their claim being that they worshipped the idols only as intercessors, and so in reality worshipped Allah. Yet the Qur'an declared them disbelievers despite that pretext.

So the scholars and jurists placed a condition on the rule: an interpretation in matters relating to the **self-evident elements of religion (Ḍarūriyyāt ud-Dīn)** must not run against their **definite (qaṭʿī)** meanings. Those are the injunctions so continuously practised, established and well known that even illiterate Muslims are aware of them: the obligation of the five daily prayers, two rakʿāt in Fajr and four in Ẓuhr, the fast of Ramadan, and likewise the prohibition of *ribā* (usury), alcoholic drinks and pig. Someone who gives false interpretations that pervert those established meanings is, by consensus of the ummah, a disbeliever — because he is in reality denying the teaching of the Prophet ﷺ. Maʿārif quotes the definition of faith recognised by that consensus: **"to believe in whatever is established to be the teaching of the Prophet ﷺ in a self-evident manner known not only to scholars, but also to the general public."**

Maʿārif also quotes **Imam Abu Yusuf** in *Kitab ul-Kharaj*: "Similar are the *zanādiqa* who deviate; and they used to pretend Islam." This, Maʿārif says, tells us that *zindīq* and *mulḥid* are one and the same — an unbeliever who outwardly claims to follow Islam but in reality refuses to obey its injunctions by distorting the meaning of the Qur'an against the explicit and definite meanings accepted by the ummah as a whole.

The most useful distinction Maʿārif ul Qurʼān gives comes from **Shah ʿAbdul-ʿAzīz Muḥaddith Dehlawī**, who sorted false interpretation into kinds:

1. Interpretation that goes against the **definite, unambiguous** texts of the Qur'an, or *mutawātir* ahadith, or the absolute consensus of the ummah — this is kufr undoubtedly.
2. Interpretation against texts that are clear and semi-certain, but **not certain or definite in absolute terms** — this is not kufr; it is *fisq* and misguidance.
3. Apart from those two, any interpretation based on a **possible understanding** of the text is the field of the jurists exercising *ijtihād*, and it carries reward from Allah in any case, as declared by a hadith.

That third level matters as much as the first. The ayah is not condemning the honest scholarly effort to understand; it is condemning the person who already knows what the Book says and sets out to make it say something else.

## Living it

**Come to the Book as a listener, not an editor.** *Ilḥād*, as the commentators describe it, begins with arriving at the Qur'an already holding a conclusion and bending the verse to fit it. Ibn ʿAbbas's phrase is a good self-check: am I putting these words in their proper place, or somewhere they do not belong?

**Take comfort in ayah 42.** Every generation produces someone confident that the Qur'an can be rewritten or explained away. Ayah 42 is Allah's own statement that both routes are sealed, and the sources point to the plain evidence: the text intact and recited worldwide, its meanings guarded, and a body of people always present to defend them.

**And hear the warning in "Do what you will."** It is not freedom; it is the warning of One who knows and sees all that we do, and who has already told us the difference between the one cast into the Fire and the one who comes secure on the Day of Resurrection.

passages.title: Nothing said to you was not said before
passages.tafsir:
These three ayat speak to a Prophet ﷺ who is being called a liar by his own people, and they steady him not with a miracle but with perspective: this has all happened before, the excuse his people offer is not their real reason, and the settling of the matter has been deferred by decree. One argument runs through all three — **rejection of revelation is an old story, it is driven by stubbornness rather than confusion, and the verdict is delayed only because a Word has already gone forth fixing an appointed term.**

## The setting: a Book nothing can get at

The verses just before this describe the Qur'an as *"an honorable well-fortified respected Book"* that falsehood cannot come to *"from before it or behind it."* Ibn Kathir explains simply that it is protected and preserved, nobody can produce anything like it, and there is no way to corrupt it, because it has been sent down by the Lord of the worlds.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān opens this out. Qatādah and As-Suddī understood *bāṭil* (falsehood) here to mean Shayṭān, and "neither from its front, nor from its behind" to mean *from any side*. Satan's manipulation and contrivance simply do not work on this Book; he cannot distort it by adding something to it or deleting something from it. The author of Tafsīr Mazharī, after quoting this, adds that "Satan" here includes the satans among jinn **and** among human beings — neither can carry out any change or distortion in the Qur'an.

Abū Ḥayyān, in *Al-Baḥr al-Muḥīṭ*, notes that the word *bāṭil* is not specific to Shayṭān: any falsehood or falsifier, from whatever source, cannot succeed against the Qur'an. Referring to Ṭabarī, he mentions an explanation Maʿārif ul Qurʼān calls "very appropriate," because there can be only two ways of introducing distortion:

- **"From its front"** — an open attempt by a disbeliever to add something to the text or delete something from it.
- **"Nor from its behind"** — a covert attempt by someone claiming to have faith to twist the *meaning* through false interpretations (*ilḥād*).

Both routes are sealed. As for the words: the Book has been read and recited throughout the world for the last fourteen centuries, fully memorised by hundreds of thousands of people, so that if anybody makes even the slightest mistake, the young, the old, the learned scholars and the unlettered — thousands upon thousands of Muslims — raise their voices for correction. As for the meaning: Maʿārif ul Qurʼān argues that Allah's undertaking *"And We are there to protect it."* (15:9) is not limited to the words only. In that verse the pronoun "it" points to the Qur'an, and the Qur'an is not just the name of words but the name of both words and meanings. So Allah has safeguarded even its meanings and injunctions, through His Messenger ﷺ and his direct disciples, the noble Companions ؓ; and whenever anyone has attempted to distort it through false explanations, thousands of scholars stand up to refute him. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān adds that it is clearly mentioned in correct ahadith that a group will always remain among the Muslims, until the Last Day, who expose the distortions of those who commit *ilḥād* and clarify the correct meaning of the Qur'an.

Ibn Kathir, on the same passage, records the meaning of *al-ilḥād*: Ibn ʿAbbās said it means "putting words in their improper places," while Qatādah and others said it means disbelief and obstinate behaviour. And of those who do it, Allah says *"they are not hidden from Us"* — which Ibn Kathir calls a stern warning and a dire threat: He knows who denies His signs, Names and attributes, and He will punish them for that.

That is the doorway into ayah 43. The Book itself is invulnerable. So the pressure falls not on the revelation, but on the man carrying it.

## "Nothing is said to you except what was said to the Messengers before you"

Qatādah, As-Suddī and others explain the sense precisely: *nothing is said to you by way of rejection and disbelief that was not said to the Messengers who came before you.* Ibn Kathir records their conclusion in two balanced clauses:

> "Just as you have been rejected, they were also rejected. Just as they bore their people's insults with patience, so too you must bear your people's insults with patience."

Notice what this does. It takes the Prophet's ﷺ private wound — the insults of his own people — and relocates it inside a pattern. The abuse is not evidence that something has gone wrong with his mission; it is evidence that his mission is like every mission before it. The mockery that felt like a verdict turns out to be a family resemblance.

And the consolation carries an instruction inside it. If the Messengers before him were rejected, then he stands in their company; and if they *bore it with patience*, then patience is what that company requires. Comfort and command arrive in the same breath. Hold on to this clause — ayah 45 will supply the historical proof for it, and repeat the command to be patient in almost the same words.

## Forgiveness and painful punishment, named side by side

Ayah 43 closes by naming two things about the Lord at once, and Ibn Kathir keeps them carefully distinct, attaching each to a different kind of person:

- **"the Possessor of forgiveness"** — "for those who turn to Him in repentance."
- **"and (also) the Possessor of painful punishment"** — "for those who persist in disbelief, transgression and stubborn opposition."

These are not two moods cancelling each other out. The same sentence that tells a persecuted Prophet ﷺ that his tormentors face painful punishment also tells him that the door of forgiveness stands open for any of them who turns back — and by the end of the passage we will learn that the reason they are still walking about un-punished is a decree, not an oversight.

## The excuse was never the reason

The argument now turns to the objectors' own reasoning and dismantles it with a hypothetical.

Ibn Kathir frames it like this: Allah tells us that the Qur'an is so eloquent and perfect in its wording and meanings, yet despite that the idolaters do not believe in it. Their disbelief, he says, is **the disbelief of stubbornness**, as Allah says elsewhere: *"And if We had revealed it unto any of the non-Arabs, and he had recited it unto them, they would not have believed in it."* (26:198–199).

So ayah 44 runs the experiment. Suppose the Qur'an had been sent as a recitation in a foreign language — what then? Out of the same stubbornness they would simply have swapped complaints: *"Why are not its verses explained in detail?"*, and by way of denunciation, *"What! not in Arabic nor an Arab?"* — meaning, as Ibn Kathir puts it, how can foreign words be revealed to an Arab who does not understand them? This interpretation was reported from Ibn ʿAbbās, Mujāhid, ʿIkrimah, Saʿīd ibn Jubayr, As-Suddī and others.

The point is devastating in its simplicity, and it is exactly what ayah 43 implied: a person who has already decided will always find a reason. The objection was never the obstacle; it was the cover story.

### Two words that look almost identical

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān, drawing on Qurṭubī, opens up a distinction that is easy to miss and changes the flavour of the taunt. Two closely related Arabic words are involved:

- **ʿajamiyy** (no hamzah at the start) — a person who is *non-Arab*; *ʿajam* means any nation other than the Arabs. Such a person may in fact speak eloquently; the word says nothing against the quality of his speech.
- **aʿjamiyy** (with a hamzah before the letter ʿayn) — the word actually used in this ayah — an Arabic term for **ineloquent speech**: a person who cannot speak eloquently.

The Qur'an chose the second. So the imagined complaint of the Quraysh — the first people addressed by this revelation — is not a mere geographical observation. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān explains that had the Qur'an been revealed in any language other than Arabic, they would have complained that they did not understand this Book, and would have said wonderingly that the prophet is an Arab but the book is *aʿjamiyy*, which is ineloquent. Their grievance would have been that revelation had come in a form they could not follow — which is precisely the excuse Allah has removed from them by sending it in Arabic, through one of their own.

## The same recitation, two receptions

Against that objection, ayah 44 gives the Prophet ﷺ a reply to say aloud: *Say: "It is for those who believe, a guide and a cure."*

Ibn Kathir: say, O Muhammad — this Qur'an, for the one who believes in it, is "guidance for his heart and a cure for the doubts and confusion that exists in people's hearts."

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān draws out both attributes:

1. **Guidance** — such guidance in all spheres of life as is beneficial and useful for human beings.
2. **Cure** — most obviously a cure for spiritual ailments: kufr, shirk, arrogance, jealousy, greed and the like. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān adds that it is also a cure for bodily ailments, as has been proved by experience of treating patients through Qur'anic prayers.

Then the other half of the ayah, on those who refuse:

- *"there is heaviness in their ears"* (**waqr**) — Ibn Kathir: they do not understand what is in it.
- *"and it is blindness for them"* — they are not guided to the explanations contained therein.

One recitation, two opposite results, as in the ayah Ibn Kathir brings here: *"And We send down of the Qur'an that which is a healing and a mercy to those who believe, and it increases the wrongdoers nothing but loss."* (17:82). The medicine is not at fault; the response to it differs. This is the same diagnosis as before — the problem is stubbornness in the listener, not obscurity in the Book.

### Called from far away

The image that ends ayah 44 is haunting: *"They are called from a place far away."*

- **Mujāhid**: "Far away from their hearts."
- **Ibn Jarīr**: "It is as if the one who is addressing them is calling to them from a distant place, and they cannot understand what he is saying."

Ibn Kathir pairs it with another Qur'anic image: *"And the example of those who disbelieve is as that of him who shouts to those (flock of sheep) that hears nothing but calls and cries. (They are) deaf, dumb and blind. So they do not understand."* (2:171).

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān, again citing Qurṭubī, shows that this is a living Arab idiom, not an abstract metaphor. To someone who understands what is being said, the Arabs say *anta tasmaʿu min qarīb* — "you are listening from a near place." To someone who does not understand the discourse, they say *anta tunādā min baʿīd* — "you are being called from a distant place." Since these people do not intend to listen and understand the directions of the Qur'an, their ears are almost deaf and their eyes are blind; teaching them the Qur'anic guidance is like calling someone from a place so distant that the voice does not reach his ears.

The distance, then, is not in the speaker and not in the volume. The Prophet ﷺ was standing right in front of them. The distance was inside them.

## Mūsā: ayah 43 proved from history

Now the frame widens once more, and the passage returns to where it began. *"And indeed We gave Musa the Scripture, but dispute arose therein."* Ibn Kathir's comment is brief and pointed: they disbelieved in him and did not show him any respect.

This is ayah 43 demonstrated. It is not merely that hard words were said to earlier Messengers as an abstract fact — a Scripture was given by Allah to Mūsā, and dispute arose over it. So the same instruction that was folded into ayah 43 is restated here in the ayah Ibn Kathir brings as the fitting response: *"Therefore be patient as did the Messengers of strong will"* (46:35).

## Why the matter has not been settled

Then comes the question that sits behind every persecution: **why does Allah not simply end it?** The ayah answers with a condition contrary to fact — *"And had it not been for a Word that went forth before from your Lord, and the matter would have been settled between them."*

Ibn Kathir explains it through the parallel wording elsewhere, *"And had it not been for a Word that went forth before from your Lord for an appointed term"* (42:14): that prior Word is the decision **to delay the Reckoning until the Day of Resurrection**. Had it not gone forth, he says, the punishment would have been hastened for them. "But they have an appointed time, beyond which they will find no escape."

So the matter is not unsettled; it is scheduled. The absence of a verdict today is not the absence of a verdict — and everyone still breathing is living inside that appointed term.

## "In grave doubt"

The final phrase is *shakk murīb* — grave, unsettling doubt. Ibn Kathir explains: their words of disbelief "are not due to any wisdom or insight on their part; rather they spoke without any attempt at examining it thoroughly." He notes this was also the interpretation of Ibn Jarīr, calls it a plausible interpretation, and closes as the scholars do where certainty is not available: "And Allah knows best."

This is the diagnosis the whole passage has been building toward, and it ties the three ayat into one. The rejectors sound confident. They produce objections about language and detail and eloquence (ayah 44). They repeat what was said to every Messenger before (ayah 43). But underneath the confidence there is no wisdom, no insight, no examination — only an unsettling doubt they never seriously tried to resolve.

## Living it

**When you are mocked for your faith, read ayah 43 as it was first heard.** It was not sent to explain your opponents to you; it was sent to steady you. The insult is old. So is the required response: bearing it with patience, exactly as the Messengers before did — the same patience ayah 45 repeats in the words *"be patient as did the Messengers of strong will"*.

**Stop trying to out-argue a person who has already decided.** Ayah 44 shows Allah answering an objection that would only have been replaced by another. Where the resistance is stubbornness rather than confusion, more argument is shouting from further away. Say your piece — the Prophet ﷺ was told *Say: "It is for those who believe, a guide and a cure"* — and leave the outcome.

**Take "a cure" literally about yourself.** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān lists the ailments the Qur'an treats: kufr, shirk, arrogance, jealousy, greed. If arrogance or envy has a grip on you, this Book is the prescription — and reciting it while ignoring the diagnosis is holding medicine you never take.

**Ask which distance you are standing at.** The idiom Qurṭubī records offers two positions: listening from a near place, or being called from a distant one. Nearness in this passage is not about how much Arabic you know — Maʿārif ul Qurʼān locates it in *intention*: these people "do not intend to listen and to understand."

**Do not mistake the delay for permission.** The only reason the matter has not been settled is a Word that went forth for an appointed term — and beyond that appointed time, Ibn Kathir says, they will find no escape. And in the very passage that names painful punishment for those who persist, Allah names Himself the Possessor of forgiveness for those who turn to Him in repentance.

passages.title: Deeds are your own when the Hour comes
passages.tafsir:
**In one breath:** these three ayat move from the most personal fact about you — that your deeds belong to you and come back to you — to the most hidden fact in creation, the timing of the Hour, and then to the moment that Hour arrives and everything a person leaned on besides Allah simply is not there.

What holds the passage together is a single idea seen from three angles: **nothing is lost, nothing is miscounted, and nothing false will survive**. Ayah 46 tells you the account is exact and just. Ayah 47 tells you the One keeping that account knows what no one else knows — down to a fruit still inside its sheath. Ayah 48 shows you the day the account is settled, when the partners people invented disappear and there is nowhere left to run.

## Ayah 46 — your deeds are yours

*"Whosoever does righteous good deed, it is for himself; and whosoever does evil, it is against himself."*

Ibn Kathir's explanation is short and pointed. On **"it is for himself"** he says: *the benefit of which will come to him*. On **"it is against himself"** he says: *the consequences of that will come back on him*.

Notice how exactly the two halves mirror each other. In both cases the deed travels, and in both cases it travels to the same address: back to the one who did it. Good work sends its benefit home to you. Wrongdoing sends its consequence home to you. The ayah does not say the good deed benefits your tribe, your family name, your reputation, or your era. It says *for himself* — and the wrong, likewise, *against himself*.

That is why this passage carries the title it does: your deeds are your own.

## "And your Lord is not at all unjust to His servants"

This is the seal on ayah 46, and it is a statement about Allah Himself. Ibn Kathir explains it in two parts, and both are worth sitting with:

**First:** *He only punishes people for their sins.* Punishment in the divine court answers precisely to what a person actually earned.

**Second:** *He does not punish anyone except after establishing proof against him and sending a Messenger to him.* This is a profound mercy embedded inside a verse about justice. Allah does not hold a person to account in the dark. Before the reckoning there is the message; before the message there is the messenger. The case is made plain first. Whatever a person then does with it, they do knowing.

And it is His own **servants** He is speaking of here — a word that already carries the relationship of a Master over those He is judging.

Hold ayah 46 together as one thought: *you get exactly what you earned, and the One who decides never wrongs anyone.* If those two are true, then the only variable left in the entire equation is what you choose to do.

## Ayah 47 — the Hour is referred back to Him alone

*"To Him is referred the knowledge of the Hour."*

Ibn Kathir's gloss is a single line, and it is total: **no one knows about that apart from Him.**

Ibn Kathir then gathers other ayat that say the same thing, so you feel this is a settled principle of the Qur'an and not a passing remark:

- *"To your Lord belongs the term thereof"* (79:44) — the end-point of the Hour belongs to Him.
- *"None can reveal its time but He"* (7:187) — no one else can uncover it.

## From the Sunnah — the leader of mankind and one of the leading angels

To show just how absolutely this knowledge is sealed, Ibn Kathir cites a moment from the life of the Prophet ﷺ. As Ibn Kathir puts it: Muhammad ﷺ, *the leader of mankind*, was asked about the Hour by Jibril, *who is one of the leading angels* — and the Prophet ﷺ answered:

> **"The one who is asked about it does not know more than the one who is asking."**

Sit with the two figures in that exchange, exactly as Ibn Kathir describes them: the leader of mankind, and one of the leading angels. If the knowledge of the Hour were going to be entrusted to any created being, these are the ones you would expect it to reach. And the answer is: *neither of us knows more than the other*. The questioner and the questioned stand on exactly the same ground.

That is what ayah 47 means when it says the knowledge is *referred to Him*. It is not that the date is hard to discover. It is that no one apart from Him knows it at all.

(The source material for this passage gives the Prophet's ﷺ words without naming the collection they come from, so the teaching is conveyed here as Ibn Kathir gives it, without attaching it to a named book of hadith.)

## Fruit in its sheath, and what a womb carries

*"No fruit comes out of its sheath, nor does a female conceive nor brings forth (young), except by His knowledge."*

Having told you what you cannot know, the ayah immediately shows you what **He** knows — and the examples chosen are not thunder and mountains. They are the quietest things in the world.

**A fruit still in its sheath.** Before it comes out, it is covered; nobody is watching it, and it may be in some grove no human has walked through. Its emergence is not outside His knowledge.

**A female conceiving, and a female giving birth.** Again the covered thing: life beginning where no eye reaches, and life emerging at a moment no one can name in advance. And note that the ayah says *a female* — not specifically a woman. The related ayah Ibn Kathir cites widens it explicitly to *every female*.

Ibn Kathir's comment on this verse: *all of that is known to Him, and nothing is hidden from your Lord the weight of a speck of dust on the earth or in the heaven.* He then lines up three more ayat that widen the same lens:

- *"Not a leaf falls, but He knows it"* (6:59) — the most ordinary event on earth, repeated uncountably, each one known.
- *"Allah knows what every female bears, and by how much the wombs fall short or exceed. Everything with Him is in due proportion"* (13:8) — not only *that* she bears, but the exact measure, the shortfall, the excess.
- *"And no aged man is granted a length of life nor is a part cut off from his life, but is in a Book. Surely, that is easy for Allah"* (35:11) — the length of every life, written; and lest you imagine such an inventory is a strain, the ayah adds that it is **easy** for Him.

Here is why this belongs in a passage about the Hour and about deeds. A person might think: *the Hour is unknown, so perhaps the whole reckoning is vague.* The ayah answers before the thought finishes forming. The One who withheld the date from you is the One who knows the fruit inside its sheath and the measure inside a womb. The timing is hidden from you; not the weight of a speck of dust is hidden from Him.

And this is exactly the knowledge that ayah 46 depends on. Perfect justice requires perfect knowledge. A judge who missed things could not be free of injustice. He is free of it — because He misses nothing.

## "Where are My partners?"

*"And on the Day when He will call unto them: 'Where are My so-called partners?' They will say: 'We inform You that none of us bears witness to it!'"*

Ibn Kathir sets the scene: this is the Day of Resurrection, and *Allah will call out to the idolators before all of creation* and say, "Where are My partners whom you worshipped besides Me?"

Two details make this scene devastating rather than merely dramatic.

**It is a call, not a private conversation.** Ibn Kathir specifies the setting: *before all of creation*. The claim was made openly in the world; it is answered openly on that Day.

**It is a question, not an accusation.** He does not say "you were wrong." He says *"Where are they?"* — and lets the silence answer. A question like this is not seeking information; it is exposing an absence. Bring them forward now. Let them stand where you said they stood.

And the answer that comes back is a total collapse of the position. They say **ādhannāka** — Ibn Kathir renders it *'we tell You'* — *"none of us bears witness to it."* Ibn Kathir's gloss on that phrase: *'not one of us will bear witness today that You have any partner.'*

Look closely at what has happened. On that Day, not a single one of them will stand up and testify that Allah has any partner. The claim does not merely lose the argument; it loses the very people who once made it.

## Ayah 48 — the vanishing, and no place to run

*"And those whom they used to invoke before shall disappear from them, and they will perceive that they have no place of refuge."*

**They disappear.** Ibn Kathir: *they will go away, and will be of no benefit to them.* There is a bitter irony worth noticing: these were the things people used to **invoke** — call upon — in this world. The one moment when calling for help actually matters is the one moment when the call finds nothing at the other end.

**And there is nowhere to go.** *"They have no place of refuge"* — Ibn Kathir: *they will have no way of escaping from the punishment of Allah.* He compares it to the scene in 18:53: *"And the criminals shall see the Fire and apprehend that they have to fall therein. And they will find no way of escape from there."*

The passage ends where ayah 46 began, only now it is seen rather than told. In ayah 46 you were informed that your evil is *against yourself*. In ayah 48 that fact becomes visible: nothing external is coming to lift it off you, because the things people invoked have gone away, and no direction leads out.

## Living it

**Take the promise of ayah 46 seriously in both directions.** Every good act, however small and however unwitnessed, is credited to *you* — the benefit comes back to you, says Ibn Kathir. Nothing you do for Allah's sake is spent into a void. And every wrong is likewise yours; its consequence comes back on you. This is a liberating thought as much as a sobering one: no one else can spend your account, and no one else can rescue it.

**Let the fruit and the womb reframe your private life.** If a fruit in its sheath is known, and what a womb carries is known by exact measure, then your hidden struggle is known, your unseen patience is known, your quiet charity is known — and so is what you do when no one is looking. Ibn Kathir's summary is worth memorising as a habit of heart: *nothing is hidden from your Lord the weight of a speck of dust on the earth or in the heaven.*

**Stop asking when, start asking what.** The Prophet ﷺ himself, asked by Jibril, said the one asked knows no more than the one asking. If Ibn Kathir's point is that no one knows the Hour apart from Allah, then the search itself is misdirected. The Qur'an redirects the energy: the timing belongs to Allah, the preparation belongs to you.

**Audit what you invoke.** Ayah 48 is not only about carved idols. It is about anything a person calls upon as if it could hold their weight before Allah. The test the ayah applies is simple and merciless: *will it still be there that Day?* Whatever fails that test is, in truth, already of no benefit — the Day only makes that plain.

**And hold on to the mercy hidden inside the justice.** The One who will ask "Where are My partners?" is the same One who, as Ibn Kathir says, *does not punish anyone except after establishing proof against him and sending a Messenger to him*. The proof has been established. The Messenger ﷺ has come. That is not a threat — it is the reason you are able to read these words and change course while the Hour is still unknown.

passages.title: Man's fickleness in ease and hardship
passages.tafsir:
These three ayat hold up a mirror. They trace one continuous portrait of the human being — tireless in asking for good, undone when hardship touches him, and then, the moment relief arrives, claiming the credit for himself and forgetting the One who gave it. Ibn Kathir gives the whole passage a single heading: **"Man is fickle when Ease comes to Him after Difficulty."** What binds ayat 49–51 together is that they follow the same person through a full cycle of ease and hardship and show that his heart never settles anywhere true.

## The shape of the passage

Ayah 49 sets the two poles: an asking for good that never tires, and a despair at evil that goes all the way down. Ayah 50 takes the same man through relief — and catches what comes out of his mouth when the pressure lifts, which turns out to be a denial of the Hour and a strange confidence that Allah owes him well in the Hereafter too; the ayah closes with Allah's answer to that confidence. Ayah 51 then runs the cycle once more in compressed form, but reverses the order — favour first, then hardship — so that the pattern is unmistakable: given, he turns his back; deprived, he will not stop calling.

Ibn Kathir reads this as a description of man, while the warning at the end of ayah 50 is aimed at "those whose conduct and belief is like that" — the disbelievers named in the ayah itself. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān, commenting on ayah 51, says plainly that "the nature of an infidel is being stated here." Both readings sit together comfortably: the disease is described in its full form in the one who denies the Hereafter, but the symptoms are familiar to anyone honest with himself.

## Ayah 49 — an asking that never tires, a despair with no floor

The ayah opens with **lā yasʾamu** — he never grows *weary*, never gets *bored*. Ibn Kathir's gloss is exactly this: "man never gets bored of asking his Lord for good things, such as wealth, physical health, etc."

Then: **wa in massahu al-sharr** — "if evil *touches* him." Ibn Kathir explains "evil" here as "trials and difficulties or poverty." And the response the ayah gives is total: **fa-yaʾūsun qanūṭ**, two words for despair stacked one on the other. Ibn Kathir's explanation of them is devastating in its simplicity: "he thinks that he will never experience anything good again."

Hold the two halves side by side and the imbalance is the whole point. Endless energy for wanting; no reserves at all for waiting. A lifetime of asking has not built in him any real conviction that the One he asks is generous, wise, and in charge.

## Ayah 50 — the words that come out when the pressure lifts

**"And truly, if We give him a taste of mercy from Us, after some adversity has touched him…"** The verb is **adhaqnāhu**, "We let him *taste*." Ibn Kathir explains it as "something good happens to him or some provision comes to him after a period of difficulty." Keep this word in mind, because the ayah will use it again at the end, and the second use is not mercy.

**"He is sure to say: 'This is due to my (merit).'"** — **hādhā lī**. Ibn Kathir unpacks the attitude behind it: "this is because of me, because I deserve this from my Lord." Yesterday he was begging; today he is an expert on his own worth. He does not say "Allah gave"; he says the outcome was owed. Ibn Kathir places alongside it:

> **"Nay! Verily, man does transgress. Because he considers himself self-sufficient."** (96:6–7)

That is the mechanism the ayah names: transgression follows on a man's seeing himself as self-sufficient. Ibn Kathir says that when this man is given a blessing "he becomes careless, arrogant and ungrateful."

**"I think not that the Hour will be established."** Ibn Kathir: "he does not believe that the Hour will come." It is worth pausing on where this sentence lands — right in the middle of good fortune.
