Ibn Kathir ties the two together directly: it is when he is given some blessing that he becomes careless and arrogant. When his life is going well, an accounting seems like someone else's problem.

**"But if I am brought back to my Lord, surely there will be for me the best with Him."** And then, in the same breath, he hedges. Ibn Kathir captures the logic: "if there is a Hereafter after all, then my Lord will be generous and kind to me just as He was in this world." He has made his worldly ease into evidence about his standing with Allah. Ibn Kathir's verdict names exactly what is missing: "he expects Allah to do him favors in spite of his bad deeds and lack of certain faith." No right deeds underneath it, and no certainty of faith — only the assumption that the arrangement he enjoys now will simply continue.

**The answer.** The ayah does not leave that assumption standing: **"Then, We verily will show to the disbelievers what they have done, and We shall make them taste a severe torment."** Two things answer him precisely. He built his case on what he *has*; he will be shown what he *did*. And the very verb of his blessing returns as the verb of his punishment — he was made to *taste* mercy, and he will be made to *taste* a severe torment. Ibn Kathir: "Thus Allah threatens punishment and vengeance to those whose conduct and belief is like that."

## Ayah 51 — the cycle run again, in reverse

**"And when We show favour to man, he turns away and becomes arrogant."** Ibn Kathir explains **aʿraḍa wa naʾā bi-jānibihi** as meaning that "he turns away from doing acts of obedience and is too proud to obey the commands of Allah." Then he sets this ordinary man's turning away beside Fir'awn's: **"But [Fir'awn] turned away along with his hosts"** (51:39). It is a sobering comparison — the same movement, named with the same kind of language, in a man whose affairs are simply going well.

**"But when evil touches him, then he has recourse to long supplications"** — **fa-dhū duʿāʾin ʿarīḍ**. Ibn Kathir notes that the "evil" here means "difficulties." This phrase deserves unpacking, because it is where the passage's finest observation lives.

**Why "broad" rather than "long"?** The word is *ʿarīḍ*, whose sense is *width*. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān notes the choice: the Qurʼān "has used the word 'broad' to describe their lengthy supplications, because what is wider will automatically be longer too," and points to how Allah uses the same word when describing Paradise — **"a paradise the width of which spans the heavens and the earth"** (3:133).

**And what fills all that space?** Ibn Kathir is blunt: "he asks at length for one thing. Long supplications are those which are long on words and short on meaning. The opposite is concise speech which is brief but full of meaning." A great deal of talk carrying very little.

**An important qualification.** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān is careful that nobody draws the wrong lesson here: "Lengthy supplications in themselves are praiseworthy and desirable," as is proved by authentic ahadith about the etiquettes of supplication, where it is mentioned that "while praying to Allah Taʿālā, beseeching tearfully and repeatedly is desirable" (Bukhari and Muslim). So the ayah is not scolding anyone for taking a long time in duʿāʼ. The censure, Maʿārif ul Qurʼān explains, "is actually not for lengthy supplications, but for his mean disposition": when Allah blesses him with wealth, honour and peace, he becomes so intoxicated with them that he grows *more* distant from the true Benefactor, and his pride and heedlessness increase; and when distress comes, he "keeps on praying in a way of wailing and complaining about his difficulties, as is the habit of heedless people; the intent is not to supplicate, but to wail about his misfortunes and to keep on telling the people about it."

That is the diagnosis, in Maʿārif ul Qurʼān's own words: the intent is not to supplicate. His broad duʿāʼ is grievance with the shape of prayer — a complaint circulated to Allah and to whoever else will listen.

Ibn Kathir seals the passage with a companion ayah that shows how the whole cycle ends:

> **"And when harm touches man, he invokes Us, lying on his side, or sitting or standing. But when We have removed his harm from him, he passes on as if he had never invoked Us for a harm that touched him!"** (10:12)

Every posture pressed into service while it hurts — then he walks on, and the entire episode leaves no trace in him. The relief that should have produced gratitude produces amnesia, which is exactly where ayah 50 began.

## Living it

The passage is a diagnostic tool. A few things it asks of a believer:

**Watch what you say when relief arrives.** *Hādhā lī* — the claim that, as Ibn Kathir puts it, "this is because of me, because I deserve this from my Lord" — is the sentence ayah 50 puts in the mouth of the man who denies the Hour. The believing alternative is accurate accounting: the taste of mercy came from Allah, and it came *after* an adversity that also came from Him.

**Do not read your comfort as a verdict.** The man in ayah 50 assumed that because his worldly life went well, "the best with Him" was waiting for him too. Ibn Kathir points out what is missing from that confidence: his bad deeds and his lack of certain faith. Ease is a test, not a report card.

**Refuse the floor-less despair of ayah 49.** "He thinks that he will never experience anything good again" is, in Ibn Kathir's description, a thought he has — and the ayah names it as a defect. The ayah of Sūrah Yūnus quoted above is the correction: it is Allah who removes the harm from him.

**Ask in ease, not only in pain.** Ayah 51 and the ayah from Sūrah Yūnus both describe someone whose duʿāʼ is a pain reflex. The cure is simple and hard: keep calling on Allah when nothing hurts.

**Make duʿāʼ deep rather than merely wide.** Taking long in supplication is praiseworthy, as Maʿārif ul Qurʼān stresses — beseeching tearfully and repeatedly is desirable. What ayah 51 exposes is prayer that is "long on words and short on meaning," and complaint dressed as worship. The test is not the length but the intent: are you truly supplicating to Allah, asking Him — or narrating your misfortune to anyone within earshot?

passages.title: Signs on the horizons and in themselves
passages.tafsir:
These three ayat bring Surah Fussilat to a close by turning the argument back on the one who refuses the Qur'an. Ibn Kathir titles this final section "The Qur'an and the Proofs of its Truth," and that is exactly what the passage delivers: first a question the rejecter is asked to answer for himself (52), then a promise that the proof he is refusing will keep arriving — from the whole universe around him and from within his own self (53) — and finally the naming of what actually lies underneath his refusal: doubt about the meeting with his Lord (54). Argument, then evidence, then the Day on which evidence will no longer be needed.

## "Tell me, if it is from Allah"

Ibn Kathir first fixes the address. *Qul* — "Say" — means, in his words, "O Muhammad, to these idolators who disbelieve in the Qur'an." Then the question itself: *ara'aytum in kana* — "Tell me, if it" — and Ibn Kathir specifies the unnamed "it": *this Qur'an*. "…is from Allah, and you disbelieve in it?"

Notice the method. The ayah does not open by proving the Qur'an. It asks the rejecter to grant the possibility for a moment and then to look at where that leaves him standing. Ibn Kathir puts the force of it plainly — the meaning is, "what do you think your position is before the One Who revealed it to His Messenger?" The sentence is deliberately left unfinished. No consequence is spelled out, because anyone honest enough to complete it has already been answered.

The other half of the ayah supplies the answer in the form of a further question: *man adallu mimman huwa fi shiqaqin ba'id* — "Who is more astray than one who is in opposition far away?" Ibn Kathir reads this as a settled condition rather than a passing mood: "he is in a state of disbelief, stubbornness and opposition to the truth, and is following a path that leads far away from guidance." Two things are named together — a posture (standing in opposition) and a direction of travel (a path leading far from guidance). So the unfinished sentence does get finished after all: if it really is from Allah and he still refuses it, then his position is that of the most astray of people.

## "We will show them Our signs"

Having asked the question, the passage does not leave the matter as a debate. It becomes a promise: *sa-nurihim ayatina fi'l-afaq wa fi anfusihim hatta yatabayyana lahum annahu'l-haqq* — "We will show them Our signs in the universe, and within themselves, until it becomes manifest to them that this is the truth."

Ibn Kathir states the purpose of these signs precisely, and it is narrower and sharper than a general call to wonder: "We will show them Our evidence and proof that the Qur'an is true and has indeed been sent down from Allah to the Messenger of Allah." The signs are evidence for one specific claim — that this Book is revelation.

**The word *afaq*.** Ma'arif ul Qur'an notes that *afaq* literally means "horizons," and that this "includes all sides of the whole universe" — which is why it is commonly translated simply as "the universe." Whatever lies out there, on any side, at the rim of what a person can see or reach, is included in the promise.

**What the outward signs are.** Ibn Kathir understands the signs "in the universe" as external signs, "such as conquests and the advent of Islam over various regions and over all other religions." He then reports from **Mujahid, al-Hasan and as-Suddi** that "signs within themselves means, the battle of Badr, the conquest of Makkah, and other events which befell them, where Allah granted victory to Muhammad ﷺ and his Companions, and inflicted a humiliating defeat on falsehood and its followers." On this reading, the proof being demanded would be delivered as events.

**And what the inward signs may be.** Ibn Kathir then preserves a second possibility rather than closing the question: "It may also be that what is meant here is man and his physical composition. As detailed in the science of anatomy, which indicates the wisdom of the Creator — may He be blessed and exalted." He includes with it "the different inclinations and opposite natures that people have, good and bad," and "the (divine) decrees to which man is subjected, having no power to change and over which he has no control."

That last item is easy to read past and is one of the sharpest signs in the passage. Ibn Kathir points to precisely what a person cannot alter and does not govern in his own life — decrees he is subject to, with no power over them. The evidence that he is a creature and not an owner is delivered to him by his own existence.

Ma'arif ul Qur'an develops this same pairing at length, and its treatment is the most vivid in the sources. Look outward first, it says: at "the creatures and creations of the whole universe, big and small, in the skies, on the earth and in between them" — and these bear witness not only to the existence of Allah, but "to His Knowledge, His all-encompassing authority, and to His being One and unique." Then it turns the reader's gaze around:

> "If one looks even nearer, at one's own self, at each organ and limb, at the fine and fragile mechanisms and systems functioning inside him to provide ease and comfort, it simply leaves one wondering."

And it gives examples a person can check on himself. These fragile mechanisms, it observes, "have been made so durable that they do not wear out even after seventy, eighty year's use." Consider the springs inside the joints: "had they been made of steel by humans, they would have been rendered unserviceable long ago." Consider the skin of the hands and the lines upon it, which "last for the whole life, and yet do not wear out."

The conclusion Ma'arif draws is modest, and stronger for being modest: a person "of even an ordinary intellect," if he genuinely ponders these matters, "is bound to believe that the Creator and Sustainer of all these things is a Being who has limitless knowledge and Authority, and there simply cannot be anyone like Him." No specialist training is required to read this evidence.

**"We *will* show them."** Ma'arif ul Qur'an makes a point about the wording that changes how the whole ayah lands. The expression is "We will show them Our signs" — and this indicates, it says, that the signs "manifested to the mankind so far are not the only signs of Allah. In fact Allah Ta'ala will continue to show His signs, both in the universe and in man's own creation, up to the Day of Judgment." The file is not closed. On this basis Ma'arif states that the ayah "covers all the new discoveries of science that man is able to reach till the end of the universe." The horizons and the self keep being opened up further, exactly as the ayah said they would be, "until it becomes manifest to them that this is the truth."

## "Is it not sufficient in regard to your Lord that He is a Witness over all things?"

The ayah ends with a question that quietly settles the argument: *a-wa lam yakfi bi-Rabbika annahu 'ala kulli shay'in Shahid*.

Ibn Kathir gives this two edges. First, it means "sufficient is Allah as a Witness over the words and deeds of His servants" — the words spoken against the Qur'an are witnessed by the very One being denied. Second, and this is a consolation to the Prophet ﷺ, "He bears witness that Muhammad ﷺ is telling the truth in what he says." Ibn Kathir supports this second sense with Allah's word elsewhere: *"But Allah bears witness to that which He has sent down unto you; He has sent it down with His knowledge"* (4:166).

So the demand for more evidence meets a decisive answer. There is a Witness whose testimony is sufficient, and He has already given it in favour of His Messenger ﷺ.

## "They are in doubt concerning the meeting with their Lord"

Ayah 54 then names what lies beneath all the arguing: *ala innahum fi miryatin min liqa'i Rabbihim* — "Lo, verily, they are in doubt concerning the meeting with their Lord."

Ibn Kathir describes this doubt as an attitude rather than an intellectual difficulty: "they doubt that the Hour will come, they do not think about it or strive for it or pay heed to it; on the contrary, they regard it as irrelevant and do not care about it." That is an honest anatomy of much rejection — not a man who has weighed the evidence and found it short, but a man for whom the question of standing before his Lord has been filed away as not applicable to him. Ibn Kathir adds the flat correction: "But it will undoubtedly come to pass."

Then the surah's final words: *ala innahu bi-kulli shay'in Muhit* — "Verily, He is surrounding all things." Ibn Kathir explains why this comes precisely here. Allah "is Able to do all things and He encompasses all things, and it is very easy for Him to bring about the Hour." Someone who doubts the Resurrection is, at bottom, doubting a capacity — so the capacity is named.

Ibn Kathir then unfolds what *muhit* carries: "all of creation is subject to His control, dominion and knowledge; He is controlling all things by His power, so whatever He wills happens, and whatever He does not will does not happen, and there is no god worthy of worship apart from Him." Control, dominion and knowledge together — and the conclusion he draws from them is not merely a statement about Allah but a claim on the servant: there is no god worthy of worship apart from Him. A surah that has been arguing about a Book ends by naming the One whose knowledge and power surround the reader on every side.

## Living it

**Take the question of ayah 52 personally.** Ibn Kathir's paraphrase is a question addressed to a person about himself: "what do you think your position is before the One Who revealed it to His Messenger?" The ayah's whole method is to make a person finish his own sentence. That is worth doing deliberately — not only by one who rejects, but by a believer whose daily life has drifted from what he claims to believe.

**Read both books of signs.** The ayah names two places — *al-afaq* and *anfusihim*. Ma'arif ul Qur'an's counsel is to look at the creations of the universe "in the skies, on the earth and in between them," and then to look "even nearer," at one's own organs and limbs, the joints, the skin of the hands. Both are Allah's signs, and Ma'arif insists that ordinary intellect is enough to be moved by them.

**Let new knowledge feed faith rather than compete with it.** Since the wording is "We *will* show them," and since Ma'arif reads the ayah as covering "all the new discoveries of science that man is able to reach till the end of the universe," a believer has no reason to meet expanding knowledge of the cosmos or the body defensively. Growing knowledge is the ayah's own prediction being fulfilled.

**Check yourself against Ibn Kathir's description of doubt.** His account of *mirya* is behavioural: not thinking about the Hour, not striving for it, not paying heed to it, regarding it as irrelevant and not caring about it. A person can apply that test to himself without arguing a single point of theology — and if the Hour has quietly become irrelevant to how his day is spent, then ayah 54 is addressing him too.

**Remember what surrounds you.** The last word of the surah is that Allah is "surrounding all things" — His control, dominion and knowledge over all creation, so that "whatever He wills happens, and whatever He does not will does not happen." For the one who doubts, that is a warning. For the one who believes, it is the ground he stands on.

*With these ayat the commentary on Surah Fussilat (Ha Mim as-Sajdah) ends. Alhamdulillah. To Allah be praise and blessings.*
